editorials.title: State of exception: On India, the UN CERD report
editorials.passage:
In its first review by the U.N. Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) since 2007, India has elicited an expression of “grave concern” about reports of the law enforcement apparatus resorting to violence — physical and otherwise — against minority ethnic and ethno-religious groups, Dalits, and non-citizens over the years. The Committee also noted that India, which ratified the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination in 1968, has not provided detailed and updated information about the state’s inquiries and sanctions arising from allegations of such violence. While the government has told CERD that caste bias falls outside Article 1 of the convention because caste is not synonymous with race, CERD has allowed all forms of discrimination based on inherited status. The Committee’s concerns also span the practice of manual cleaning of sewers despite a law banning it; hate speech against, poor living conditions of, and the mass refoulement of Rohingya Muslims; the mass deprivation of citizenship via the National Register of Citizens; large-scale deletions from the Special Intensive Revisions of electoral rolls; the government’s use of the FCRA, UAPA, AFSPA, and PMLA instruments to hamper the work of civil society organisations; the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita not expressly criminalising racist hate speech; and the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act exempting “national security” projects from consultative decision-making.

Given these issues and the fragmented recourse available, the lack of suitably disaggregated data on disenfranchised communities, including due to a much-delayed Census and the slow release of NCRB data, has transcended the bounds of administrative lethargy to actively impeding independent checks of India’s claims about fighting caste- and faith-based discrimination. In fact, India has been implementing “special measures” based on 2011 Census data, which could mask a regression in the socioeconomic status of Scheduled Tribes and Adivasis. Together with the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions recommending the downgrade of the NHRC last year, following the government appointing police officers to investigative roles and a lack of pluralism, CERD is effectively stepping into a vacuum. The road ahead remains clear, from restoring the NHRC’s independence and criminalising hate speech to supportive affirmative action, collecting and publishing disaggregated data, and improving the transparency of the electoral roll revisions, and strengthening enforcement overall. But if the government’s attempted use of a technicality to keep the issues of 200 million Dalits a “domestic matter” and avoid international accountability — and its dismissal of CERD’s concerns as politically motivated — is any guide, the task continues to fall to civil society to exert influence in multilateral fora and sustain political, legal, and administrative resistance to government choices that normalise India’s sadly widespread culture of discrimination of all sorts.

editorials.title: Drawn to defeat: On India’s chances in the ICC World Test Championship
editorials.passage:
This was a triumph that ironically suffered the after-effects of a loss. India’s 1-0 series victory in the two-Test outing recently in Sri Lanka, in normal circumstances, would have been seen as a positive. However, in the race for key points in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) cycle, the ideal India-centric result would have been a clean sweep at 2-0. But with Dhananjaya de Silva’s men thwarting India’s bid for a win in the second Test at Colombo’s Sinhalese Sports Club Ground, and forcing a draw, the visitors continue to occupy the fifth slot in the WTC rankings. It is a position one below Bangladesh after the eastern neighbour secured a 1-1 draw against Australia in the series Down Under. If a WTC final berth has to be secured then India has to do extremely well away against New Zealand and at home against Australia, and then hope that the various permutations cropping up will be favourable. Shubman Gill’s men find themselves in this piquant situation due to their vulnerability at home, having lost a Test series to South Africa last year. The transition angst within the Indian unit is yet to abate following the exit of R. Ashwin, Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma. Slowly, new heroes are emerging and the results could improve.

Stepping into the Emerald Isle and hamstrung by the injured Jasprit Bumrah’s absence, India did its homework. A warm-up fixture was won, while some of its players had earlier turned out for India A against Sri Lanka A and were ready. When the series commenced with the first Test at picturesque Galle, India led from the front and won by 165 runs to secure a 1-0 lead. Devdutt Padikkal’s 167 and 44 led the run charts and most importantly it also meant that the critical number three spot in the batting order had found an apt occupant for now. This is the same position that in the past had featured pedigreed men such as Dilip Vengsarkar, Rahul Dravid and Cheteshwar Pujara. Left-arm spinner Manav Suthar too did well and his classical mode is a throwback to a gentle past. Sri Lanka’s brief resistance hinged on Sonal Dinusha, who registered a ton. Soon he would become an immovable personality at the batting crease and India learnt it the hard way at Colombo. His twin hundreds helped Sri Lanka erase the ignominy of suffering a follow-on and also survive a tense final day to wrest a draw. The conclusion felt like a victory for the host and India is now placed in a must-win corner in its future Tests.

editorials.title: Warning labels are only the first step against junk food
editorials.passage: After the Supreme Court directed the government to introduce health warning labels on the front of junk food packets and drink bottles, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pledged to follow through on it. On Friday, the regulator proposed mandating hexagonal labels for products high in saturated fat, sugar, or salt—similar to warnings required in dozens of other countries. It’s worrying that India, where the National Institute of Nutrition has warned for years about excessive amounts of these ingredients in ultra-processed food, took so long to act. In July, the Indian Council of Medical Research formed the Let's Fix Our Food consortium to raise awareness that such ingredients increase the risk of diabetes and other non-communicable diseases. But it took a nudge from the top court for the government to finally agree to the measure.This raises the unsavoury question of whether successive Indian governments have allowed a lower safety standard for food and drinks sold in the country. Two years ago, when regulators in Singapore and Hong Kong stopped sales of packaged masalas from two top Indian brands because of unsafe amounts of a cancerous pesticide, rather than ordering extensive testing at home, the government only informed the Rajya Sabha that the hazard was limited to a few batches. The image of a health warning stuck on a packet of Indian Maggi sold in California caused alarm on Indian social media. Last week’s report that a bottle of the fizzy drink Fanta sold in Delhi contains thrice as much sugar as it does in London attracted caustic comments from food influencers online..Now that the FSSAI has agreed to front-of-pack warning labels, it must make them understandable to all Indians. To “facilitate informed food choices”, as its court filing promised, the regulator must ask companies to print legible warnings about recommended daily portions. A scannable QR code can provide access to more information in all Indian languages.A recent study published in The Lancet estimated that as many as 45 crore Indians could be obese or overweight by 2050. Expensive weight-loss drugs are increasingly eating into household budgets across the country. editorials.title: Congress risks paying for internal discord
editorials.passage: The Congress government in Telangana is facing an avoidable political problem. Opposition criticism is part of democratic politics. More damaging, however, are controversies arising from within the ruling party, which inevitably provide its opponents with fresh ammunition.The latest episode involving Endowments Minister Konda Surekha has again brought this into focus. Her daughter publicly expressed displeasure after Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy reportedly promised the Parkal Assembly seat, which she had sought, to another leader. The controversy has acquired greater significance in the context of earlier episodes involving the minister and her family. Reports that the party’s disciplinary committee has recommended action against Surekha indicate that the leadership views the matter seriously.Nor is this an isolated instance of internal differences spilling into the public domain. Chinna Reddy’s allegation that Assembly tickets were sold for crores of rupees is another example. Whatever its immediate political context, such a charge inevitably has consequences beyond the local rivalry that may have prompted it.As the Congress government approaches its third year in office, these distractions come at an inopportune time. It is already facing criticism over issues such as the controversy surrounding Section 22A and the inclusion of private properties in the prohibited list. Internal discord can only add to its difficulties..Political parties need space for differences and dissent. But when disagreements repeatedly become public spectacles, they affect both the party and the government. The Congress leadership will have to deal with such matters with political sensitivity, taking into account the influence and constituencies of individual leaders while also preserving organisational coherence.The larger issue is not the resolution of one controversy but the impression created by a succession of them. The Telangana Congress would do well to ensure that internal contests do not distract attention from governance and the agenda on which it sought and received the people’s mandate..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | Winged instrusion
editorials.passage: Germans were scratching their heads recently, wondering how a bunch of mosquitoes had entered their airspace, probably as stowaways aboard a flight, and infected six workers at Frankfurt Airport. Two died. For a country that had forgotten malaria, authorities suddenly had to dust off treatment protocols. They set traps to catch the intruders. If caught, the mosquitoes will be tested to establish their species and origin. For Frankfurt, it’s a case of once bitten, twice shy after a similar run-in in 2023. India should take note. Eradicating malaria by 2030 will be a major achievement, but keeping it out may prove just as important. editorials.title: The Control in the Age of Algorithmocracy
editorials.passage:
For the majority of history, the character of politics was evident in the forms of power. It was the king on the throne, the emperor in the palace, the dictator running the state, or the ruling class commanding the army and bureaucracy. No matter the construction of the state, designations of sovereignty were known. Jean Bodin’s definition of sovereignty as “supreme authority over a territory” was indicative of this framework.

Democracy was one of the most significant events to occur in the history of political thought. While previously power was in the hands of individuals or ruling classes, with democracy sovereignty resided with the people. Legitimacy began to reside with popular will, and the vote was the means of expressing sovereignty. Rousseau famously stated that “the sovereign has no other name than the people.”

In contrast, a new development is in process that is less about a new political system and more about a new locus of influence. Control over the data, the algorithms, the means of information, and the processing systems makes it possible to control the information environment in which citizens form their beliefs and opinions and in which they make their decisions.

This is the riddle of Algorithmocracy.

Rather than only asking who has the power to govern, we are now asking who has the power to control the systems through which people see, make sense of, and act upon the world.

Algorithms don't produce legal frameworks or regulations, mobilize the army, or manage a country. However, algorithms create the content we see, engage with, and, ultimately, ignore. Algorithms influence our decisions and our behavior without even giving us answers. In fact, a seemingly passive algorithm is enough to dictate what we see.

Nate Persily from Stanford holds that large technology companies have the most power over their respective information ecosystems since the pre Reformation Catholic church. While the reference point might sound strange, Persily points out an important dimension of modern structural power. Contemporary structural power does not deal with the power over the information flow. Rather, it is about the power over information visibility, position, repetition, and dissemination.

Do you ever get recommendations based on a conversation you had with your friend through WhatsApp on another social media app? While it might not have 'read' your private conversation, the data economy logic is that the data/signals of our digital lives indicate what interests us.

Whenever you send a WhatsApp message, post a selfie, like a post, type a Google search, transact something using UPI, or engage with an AI chatbot in any other way, you are adding to the enormous volume of data through which machines learn how humans behave.

We are producing data constantly, but we often don't think about ourselves as data producers.

The cycle is remarkable. Data are processed by algorithms, algorithms influence our attention, attention affects our perception, and perception influences our behavior. That behavior, in turn, produces more data.

<strong>Behavior Data Algorithms Attention Perception Behavior</strong>

Machines are no longer merely observational. They have become active participants in the cycles they observe. They respond to the data they collect and influence the behavior that generates further data.

This makes Algorithmocracy self-reinforcing.

Greater interaction with digital systems produces more data. More data can generate more accurate predictions. More accurate predictions enable increasingly personalized attention. At that point, the volume of behavioral data can expand dramatically.

The more important question, therefore, is not simply who owns the data.

It is who controls the intelligence extracted from it.

This may become one of the defining political dilemmas of the digital age.

An individual search may reveal very little. Millions of searches, however, can reveal the anxieties of an entire society. One purchase may tell us almost nothing. Millions of transactions can reveal consumption patterns. One political preference may remain private, but thousands of behavioral signals can reveal the environment in which preferences are formed.

Data are not merely a diary of history.

Data are a means of predicting the present and the future.

Consequently, competition among major technology companies is moving beyond users, attention, advertising and market share. It is increasingly centered on data, algorithms and computing, the fundamental building blocks of artificial intelligence.

In the US, companies within the FAANG or FAMGA model include Google, Facebook, Amazon, Apple and Netflix. These companies, along with many others, have built global, privately held services. In China, companies known as the BATX model (Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent and Xiaomi) have built their services in a state-aligned digital ecosystem. China recognized data as a fundamental factor of production alongside land, labor, capital and technology. As such, they consider data a strategic national resource.

While the US’s model continues to be corporate-centric, technology companies are beginning to work alongside the government in fields like cloud computing and defense. However, it is more complicated than a state vs. private system distinction. Both integrate the commercial and strategic interests.

Data are non-rival and can be appropriated many times in many forms. Because data is socially produced, it can contribute to new and more complex knowledge. Competition for data is becoming geopolitical, along with computing and AI capabilities and semiconductor supply chains. Thus, digital sovereignty, data localization, and the establishment of digital infrastructure and service standards also become major strategic concerns.

Unlike the West’s corporate-centric model, and unlike China’s state-centric model, India is attempting to develop a model that incorporates a Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) as universal civic digital utilities, that neither completely centralizes nor allows private monopolies to control digital systems.

Large-scale digital infrastructures have been developed with the implementation of systems like Aadhaar and UPI. UPI has facilitated more than 10 billion transactions a month. AI and the IndiaAI Mission are also likely to enable secure and sovereign AI growth by building computing infrastructure, data and AI services.

Building digital infrastructure while providing oversight and ensuring security for citizens and preventing global technology companies from undermining digital self-reliance is challenging.

All of this circles back to the major political concern: who is sovereign?

In most cases, sovereignty has been either with the king or queen in a monarchy or with the people and is exercised through the democratic process in a democracy. In the information age, there are other forms of informal shadow sovereignty along with traditional political systems and institutions. Although they are not law-makers, they can control the informational domain in which public opinion and decision-making occur.

Algorithmocracy has not superseded democracy, but rather has created a new co-existent power beside it.

Algorithms are the mechanics, while data is the fuel.

Since in the past political power was proportional to strategic resources, it is likely the next great political and geostrategic competition may not be about who owns the algorithms, but rather who controls the data that empowers it.

<em>(The author holds a PhD in International Relations from JNU)</em>

editorials.title: Uneasy reckoning
editorials.passage:
There exists a particular species of consensus that is born not of deliberation but of attrition ~ the moment an institution abandons the question of whether a force can be resisted and resigns itself instead to the narrower, more manageable question of how it might be tamed. India’s education establishment appears to have arrived at exactly such a threshold with artificial intelligence, and its clearest articulation, fittingly, issued from the country’s highest judicial chair. 

Addressing the Vice-Chancellors’ Conclave at the National Law University, Jodhpur, earlier this month, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant advanced a position that would have seemed almost heretical a decade ago and now reads as quietly self-evident: that India’s law schools must relinquish any impulse toward prohibition and instead admit generative AI into the classroom on their own terms. Technology, he observed, was no longer rapping tentatively at the profession’s door but had already colonised its innermost chambers ~ legal research, contract drafting, due diligence, the very choreography of dispute resolution. 

What lends the Chief Justice’s intervention its true weight is not simply its content but its unflinching candour. He did not gloss over the perils. Students, he cautioned, risked lapsing into dependence upon outputs that sounded persuasive yet stood on unsound legal footing, their faculty for independent reasoning withering imperceptibly beneath the seduction of convenience. And yet his prescription was not retreat but discipline of a different order ~ that law schools instil in their students not mere technological fluency, but the finer art of discernment: knowing when a tool may assist, when it must be interrogated, and when it must be set aside altogether in deference to human judgment. 

It is a formulation of considerable precision, and, in the same breath, a tacit confession that the guardrails ~ if they are to exist at all - must be erected while the vehicle is already hurtling forward. The Union Budget for 2026-27 accorded the Ministry of Education an allocation exceeding Rs. 1.39 lakh crore, with the Department of School Education and Literacy receiving its most generous outlay in history ~ upward of Rs. 83,500 crore ~ accompanied, notably, by a mandate to constitute a High-Powered Committee charged with examining how artificial intelligence will recast the contours of employment and skill, and with charting its integration across every rung of the educational ladder. 

The IndiaAI Mission, envisaged with an outlay surpassing Rs. 10,000 crore, has already enlisted tens of thousands of GPUs into service and shortlisted teams to construct indigenous foundational language models ~ an infrastructural undertaking of such magnitude that it betrays the state’s conviction: this is no experiment to be observed cautiously from the margins, but an inevitability to be engineered with deliberate haste. The National Education Policy of 2020 had, in truth, already laid the philosophical scaffolding years before generative AI entered common parlance ~ envisioning a National Educational Technology Forum and a curriculum emancipated from the rigidity of disciplinary silos, supple enough to absorb whatever technological insurgency the coming decades might yet produce. 

What is unfolding today, then, is less a rupture with that earlier vision than its abrupt and somewhat breathless fulfilment. Beneath these commanding, macro-level pronouncements, the transformation is being enacted in far more modest surroundings. Educators at the coalface ~ lecturers, placement officers, department heads ~ speak not of wholesale substitution but of a recalibration of emphasis: AI conscripted as an assistant, summoned to simplify, to draft, to furnish a serviceable first pass, while the labour of judgment, originality and genuine comprehension s expected to remain the inviolable preserve of the human mind. 

It is a reassuring distinction, intoned with almost liturgical regularity across classrooms and blog posts alike. But reassurance is not the same currency as certainty, and the boundary between assistance and dependency is precisely the one the Chief Justice himself identified as perilously fine - easily blurred, and more easily forgotten. It would be a mistake to read the Chief Justice's remarks as merely rhetorical, for they sit atop a legal and constitutional lineage far older than the technology now testing it. 

The Constitution’s Fundamental Duties, in Article 51A(h), enjoin every citizen to cultivate a scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry and reform ~ a clause drafted decades before anyone could have foreseen a machine capable of simulating inquiry itself, yet one that reads today as an uncanny anticipation of precisely the discernment the CJI was demanding of India's law graduates. 

The right to education, whether traced through Article 21A’s explicit guarantee for children or the wider penumbra the courts have read into Article 21 for higher learning, further binds any expansion of AI in classrooms to a constitutional promise of access ~ a promise that Article 14's guarantee of equality renders uneasy, given how unevenly the infrastructure of artificial intelligence is likely to reach India’s urban law schools before it reaches its district colleges. At the regulatory level, the architecture remains deliberately unfinished. 

The University Grants Commission's 2023 circular directed higher education institutions merely to remain vigilant and to devise their own internal safeguards against AI misuse, setting no uniform threshold ~ leaving India’s universities to legislate, in effect, upon themselves. This restraint is not accidental. It mirrors, almost exactly, the philosophy embedded in the India AI Governance Guidelines unveiled by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology in November 2025: a consciously “light-touch,” techno-legal approach that declines to lead with prohibition, choosing instead to lean upon existing law, sectoral judgment, and institutional discretion. Here, then, lies the uncomfortable symmetry worth dwelling upon. 

A nation is, in the same breath, channelling unprecedented capital into AI infrastructure, weaving the technology into the very constitutional imagination of its national curriculum, and being counselled by its most senior jurist against banning it even within a discipline erected entirely upon the discipline of unaided thought ~ while conceding, almost as an aside, that the very technology it embraces may erode the faculties it purports to sharpen. This is not so much contradiction as it is wager: a considered bet that supervision, ethics and pedagogy can be assembled with sufficient speed and rigour to outpace a technology whose capabilities compound faster than any curriculum committee can convene to deliberate upon them. 

Every generation of Indian education has, in its turn, absorbed some disruptive innovation and emerged, eventually, the more capable for it ~ the printing press, the calculator, the search engine. Each time, the anxious question was the same: would the tool think for the students, or merely think alongside them? Artificial intelligence is not the first such reckoning to visit India’s classrooms. It may, however, be the first to arrive at a velocity that affords little of the customary luxury ~ those unhurried decades in which earlier technologies were permitted to be cautiously, deliberately domesticated. 

(The writer is Lecturer, Faculty of Law, IIM Rohtak)

editorials.title: Sweet and sour
editorials.passage:
India’s sugar squeeze is exposing a policy problem that goes well beyond the price of sweets. The immediate concern is whether enough sugar will be available at reasonable prices during the festive season. The more consequential question is whether India’s pursuit of energy security is beginning to collide with its obligation to protect food security. Sugar production has fallen well below earlier expectations, while domestic consumption remains close to the country’s total output. 

Yet India allowed substantial exports before the scale of the shortfall became clear and has now opened the door to duty-free imports of up to one million tonnes ~ the first such move in nearly a decade. The reversal is striking: a country that had been exporting sugar is now bringing it in to protect domestic supplies. Weather provides part of the explanation. Sugarcane is exceptionally dependent on water, and erratic rainfall, dry spells, excessive rain and disease have damaged crops in important producing states. Hoarding and speculative buying may also have aggravated the price surge. But these factors do not fully explain the policy failure. When production estimates can prove so optimistic that exports are authorised and imports become necessary within the same season, the credibility of the forecasting system itself must be questioned. This is where E20 enters the debate. 

It would be simplistic to claim that ethanol caused the sugar shortage. The government says the share of cane diverted to ethanol has fallen. E20 also serves legitimate energy-security objectives. But E20 has created a competing demand for the same agricultural resource. Cane can ultimately support either sugar production or ethanol production. In years of abundant harvests, that trade-off may be manageable. In a poor crop year, however, diverting millions of tonnes of sugar equivalent to ethanol reduces the cushion available to absorb a production shock. That distinction matters. E20 may not have caused this crisis, but it has made the consequences of a supply miscalculation more serious. India therefore needs to stop treating food security, energy policy and agricultural trade as separate silos. 

India cannot encourage cane diversion to fuel, permit exports on optimistic projections and then respond to shortages with imports without examining how those policies interact. It suggests that those in charge took their eye off the ball. The answer is not necessarily to abandon E20. It is to build flexibility into the transition. When sugar production forecasts fall sharply, ethanol allocations should be capable of adjustment. When stocks approach a predetermined safety threshold, exports should automatically become more restrictive. 

Crop estimates should be independently scrutinised before export permissions are expanded. And strategic sugar reserves should be treated as seriously as the country’s other food-security buffers. The larger warning is simple: energy security cannot be pursued by pretending that food security has no opportunity cost. India needs E20 to work without making its kitchens pay for mistakes made in forecasting, trade policy or agricultural planning.

editorials.title: A woman’s voice
editorials.passage:
The uproar over women using profanity at political protests says rather more about Indian society than it does about bad language. The real discomfort appears to arise when young women refuse to behave according to the conventions expected of them ~ and do so publicly, angrily and without apology. There is nothing particularly novel about Indians swearing. 

Political discourse, television debates, cinema and social media have long demonstrated how casually abusive language has entered public life. Men in politics have hurled personal insults at opponents, sometimes even inside Parliament, without the nation pausing to ask whether their upbringing or character has been compromised. Yet when young women use similar language in a political confrontation, the discussion quickly becomes one about morality, culture and how women ought to conduct themselves. That double standard deserves scrutiny. There is, of course, a legitimate argument against political abuse. 

Profanity can cheapen disagreement, turn argument into intimidation and make public discourse coarser. A protester does not acquire an unlimited right to insult someone merely because the protest concerns a legitimate grievance. Democratic politics depends upon the ability to distinguish fierce criticism from personal degradation. But precisely the same standard must apply to everyone. If a young man abuses a political leader, the response should be about the abuse. If a young woman does exactly the same thing, it should not suddenly become a referendum on womanhood. Once the language of “our daughters” enters the argument, the issue has changed. 

The implicit demand is no longer simply that citizens behave responsibly; it is that women remain within a narrower boundary of acceptable public behaviour. That boundary has consequences far beyond profanity. Women who participate in contentious politics routinely discover that criticism of their ideas can rapidly become attacks on their sexuality, appearance, family and personal lives. Online harassment, sexual abuse, threats and attempts to expose private information are not legitimate extensions of political disagreement. They are mechanisms of intimidation. 

This is particularly significant as a younger generation enters politics through social media. Its political vocabulary is often irreverent, visual and deliberately provocative. That style can be immature and occasionally offensive. But dismissing it as merely uncivil misses the larger transformation: young citizens, including women, increasingly see no reason why political authority should automatically command deference. The answer cannot be to romanticise profanity. Nor should it be to demand that women earn political legitimacy by remaining more decorous than men. 

India needs a genuinely equal standard of public conduct. Abuse should be condemned whether it comes from a protester, a minister, an MP, a television anchor or a party worker. At the same time, women must be allowed the same political anger, irreverence and freedom to challenge authority that men have traditionally claimed. The deeper test of a democracy is not whether its citizens always speak politely. It is whether the same rules apply when they do not.

editorials.title: Intent to harm
editorials.passage:
What is emerging from the case against Meta, which consolidated lawsuits brought by 29 state attorneys general in the United States of America, is a landmark judicial exploration of the notion of malign intent in a social media operation. Although the hearings ended in a settlement within days of having begun in Oakland, California, this month, the revelations following a nationwide investigation that began in 2021 are quite mind-boggling.

The first claim against Meta involves exploitative and addictive product design: that it engineered features designed to exploit vulnerabilities associated with adolescent development and to maximise engagement. And that it continued to deploy these features even after its own internal research documented links between Instagram use and harms to young users, including depression, anxiety and body-image concerns among them. The Conversation reported that internal documents cited in the lawsuit allege Meta studied adolescent brain development (including aspects such as lower impulse control and high reward sensitivity) and tailored its products to maximise the length of time users spent on platforms. That itself is pretty damning.

Social media, as we know by now, thrives on maximising engagement.

In 2012, Facebook saw its teen audience decline for the first time ever and bought Instagram. Under it, the app grew rapidly. But by 2018, several external studies were establishing a link between social media apps and rising rates of mental health issues among teens. That the company was aware of the scrutiny Instagram was coming under in this regard becomes clear from “ The Facebook Files ” , a series The Wall Street Journal published in 2021. It said it was based on a review of internal Facebook documents, including research reports, online employee discussions and drafts of presentations to senior management. It showed that Facebook’s researchers identified the ill-effects of the platforms on the real world, and that despite congressional hearings and media exposés and much else, the company did not fix them.

Employees raised alarms about the harmful ways in which Facebook’s platforms were being used in developing countries, where its user base was huge and expanding. Employees also flagged that human traffickers in the Middle East used the site to lure women into abusive employment situations, and armed groups in Ethiopia used the site to incite violence against ethnic minorities. They also highlighted organ selling, pornography and government action against political dissent. But the company did very little about any of this, the series says.

Another set of claims concerns Meta’s collection of data from children under 13 without parental consent, allegedly in violation of a federal children’s privacy law. And the states argued that these practices violated state consumer protection statutes as well. The consumer protection claim is particularly important. For decades, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act has protected platforms from liability for content posted by their users. But the states sued Meta instead over the company’s own product design, business practices and alleged misrepresentations, not for user-generated content.

California’s lawyer has been widely quoted for her opening argument. In it, she compressed the theory into four keywords: Meta’s business model, she said, was to “hook” users, “hold” them, “harvest” their data and “hide” the harm. And there was already precedent at the state level, in Massachusetts , of courts allowing this kind of claim to proceed.

The company’s own announcement says that the agreement reached in Oakland includes a payment of approximately $18 billion, which can be used to fund youth online safety initiatives, among other state priorities. Distributed in annual instalments over a 10-year period, participating states will receive approximately 70% of the allocated payment over the decade. Mark Zuckerberg has inserted a parting kick though — the remaining 30% (approximately $5.3 billion) will be released only after its rivals, YouTube and TikTok, also implement a one-hour daily limit, night mode, and age assurance measures, and YouTube and TikTok each pay an amount matching the 30% figure, with half of the remaining funds tied to YouTube’s payment and half-tied to TikTok’s. This is about Meta, but Meta wants it to be also about TikTok and YouTube.

Even though it is quibbling about the manner in which it will pay, the money is a pittance for Meta, as it is for any of the other platforms.

What changes with this lawsuit is that it is no longer about whether or not a platform has safe harbour for user content that it hosts. It is now about Meta being required to redesign Facebook and Instagram to curb their addictive features. The design changes, such as curbing infinite scroll and autoplay, are the substantive core of the agreement. Teens under 18 on Instagram and Facebook in the US and in countries abroad will now encounter blocks and controls which will change the default experience rather than simply adding another setting that users can choose to activate. Some eight measures have been specified. But how all of this will actually work calls for a sense of realism. Meta is an old player, and did not reach where it has by being either ethical or law-abiding.

This Meta settlement has been described by public interest groups as a missed opportunity for public accountability. A trial would have afforded a rare opportunity for Meta investors to see Zuckerberg answer probing questions under oath. In 2017, Zuckerberg was expected to testify at a trial involving a lawsuit by company investors opposed to his plan to issue a special class of Facebook stock that would have extended his control over that company. That case was also settled before he took the stand.

In July 2025, the company had settled with shareholders who had sued Zuckerberg and current and former directors and officials of Meta Platforms for the damage they allegedly caused the company by allowing repeated violations of Facebook users’ privacy. The shareholders wanted the 11 defendants to use their personal wealth to reimburse the company, but it was Meta Platforms which settled the claims for $8 billion.

A settlement also forecloses something else: the public records of evidence that trials produce. The internal documents and testimony surfacing in Oakland, including evidence about Meta’s own research on young users and its lawyers’ handling of those findings, will now remain only partially on record.

The tailpiece from India on young users is most ironic. In July this year, a BBC Eye investigation found that Instagram has been running paid adverts promoting child sexual abuse material in India, and directing viewers to Telegram where these videos could be bought. First, Instagram told the BBC that the post did not violate its “community guidelines”. Action from the relevant ministry following this report was to order a takedown. The BBC created an alias account and found that the ads surfaced again. Nobody has reported that any case was lodged against Instagram for running such advertising or that any fine was levied.

When the Parliamentary Stan­ding Committee on Comm­uni­cations and Information Tech­no­logy grilled Meta officials earlier this month regarding the temporary removal of a video by the prime minister, Narendra Modi, from Facebook and demanded an apology from Zuckerberg, it also accused the platform of failing to act effectively against child sexual abuse material and content affecting women. It is not clear if the subject of Instagram running ads for pornographic videos came up at all; reports of the closed-door meeting do not mention it.

Sevanti Ninan is a media commentator, and was founder editor of TheHoot.org. She runs the Worker Web newsletter on Substack, and a WhatsApp channel of the same name

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Food diktat misreads Durga Puja’s cultural fabric
editorials.passage:
Sir — The Vishwa Hindu Parishad recently met organisers of Durga Puja in the city and issued some diktats, including restricting non-vegetarian food in and around pandals in West Bengal (“Not for all”, Aug 30). The VHP claims that Durga Puja is a religious festival and non-vegetarian food would contaminate its “sanctity and cleanliness”. However, fish and mutton are not just traditional staples at Bengali feasts but also served to the goddess in some shakta and tantric traditions. Attempting to enforce a strictly vegetarian mandate misreads the cultural fabric of the festival and the region.

Sir — A controversy has erupted over the forthcoming publication of Sonia Gandhi’s memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love . Congress leaders have alleged that Penguin Random House India faced pressure to remove passages concerning the prime minister, Narendra Modi, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and Chinese incursions from the book. PRHI has disputed this, stating that it is not the book’s Indian publisher and that reports linking its decision to proposed editorial changes are inaccurate. The Congressman, Ashok Gehlot, has rightly asked why material being published internationally should face obstacles in India. The dispute has thus raised a broader question about freedom of expression. Fact-checking and editorial scrutiny should not become censorship.

Jang Bahadur Singh, Jamshedpur

Sir — PRHI’s recent decisions have invited concern that its editorial judgement is yielding to political caution. The publisher withdrew plans to distribute Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot , an account of the 2013 Muzaffarnagar riots, in India. General M.M. Naravane’s memoir, Four Stars of Destiny , also remains unpublished, although PRHI retains its publishing rights. Its catalogue, meanwhile, includes works sympathetic to the ruling establishment and its ideological affiliates, creating an appearance of uneven editorial standards. Sonia Gandhi has repeatedly faced personal abuse, derogatory allegations and misleading material in political discourse and online. Her memoir could provide an opportunity to answer such attacks in her own words. Publishers play an important role in sustaining informed public debate; repeated retreats from politically sensitive works risk damaging their credibility and reputation.

Aayman Anwar Ali, Calcutta

Sir — The controversy around Sonia Gandhi’s has inadvertently generated considerable publicity for it. PRHI has fallen in public estimation over its handling of the matter. Sonia Gandhi’s refusal to accept the reported changes reflects her defence of authorial freedom and the public’s right to know.

G. David Milton, Maruthancode, Tamil Nadu

Sir — Sudhanva Desh­pande, the editor of Left­Word, offered a persuasive assessment of the controversy: “From the outside, it doesn’t appear to me that the government is trying to arm-twist Penguin. It appears to me that Penguin is doing this voluntarily.” Much like several media organisations that practise anticipatory compliance. PRHI’s decision reflects editorial timidity and possible self-censorship. Sonia Gandhi’s memoir could serve as a valuable political record, given that she has witnessed several decades of profound change in Indian and global politics.

Bidyut Kumar Chatterjee, Faridabad

Sir — Three incidents across the country raise serious questions about Indian authorities’ commitment to public safety. First, a Class I student was bitten by a snake on the premises of a government-run school in Calcutta (“City school snakebite”, Aug 25). He was subsequently reported to be in a stable condition. In Amravati, Maharashtra, three newborn babies died after a ventilator reportedly caught fire in the neonatal intensive care unit of the government-run District Women’s Hospital. In the third incident, a rat bit a passenger on the nose aboard the Una Himachal-Indore Express. These incidents expose serious deficiencies in maintenance, sanitation and safety protocols at public institutions and on public transport.

Sir — A child being bitten by a snake on a Calcutta school campus is alarming. A similar incident at another school only days earlier suggests that the danger cannot be dismissed as an isolated accident. It raises an obvious question: why did the first incident not prompt wider preventive action? Snakes pose a foreseeable risk during the monsoon, particularly near open spaces and wetlands. Regular inspections of vegetation, drains, toilets and waste-disposal areas, along with a clear emergency-response plan, should be mandatory in every school.

A.K. Mookherjee, North 24 Parganas

Sir — India has a large agrarian population, and venomous snakebites claim many lives in villages. During the monsoon, snakes often seek shelter on higher or drier ground, increasing the risk to adults and children alike in rural areas.

editorials.title: Grey fields
editorials.passage:
The United Nations has declared 2026 as the International Year for Rangelands and Pastoralists to boost policy support for pastoralism and rangeland management. Rangelands include grasslands, forbs, shrubs and fauna grazed by livestock and wildlife. Pastoralists are key custodians of these landscapes, contributing to food security while preserving ecosystems, cultural heritage and indigenous knowledge. These two phenomena give rise to transhumance, or seasonal droving of humans with livestock between varying geographic and climatic regions. Transhumance has long been castigated in India, though nomadic tribes like Gujjars, Bakkerwals and Gaddis offer invaluable ecosystem services.

Transhumant pastoralists enter the public eye only when they disrupt traffic. In Jammu and Kashmir and Uttarakhand, semi-nomadic herders move during summer from the plains to higher reaches seeking climate and fodder suitable for their cattle. With the onset of winter, they stride downhill with their flocks. More than six lakh herdsmen embark on this harrowing biannual trek and help prevent forest fires. Due to stereotyping, their minuscule population and migratory lifestyle, the rights of Himalayan pastoralists have been ignored, marginalising these communities. Many have blamed the herdsmen for overgrazing and dwindling livestock. Yet the theory of Himalayan degradation due to overgrazing and soil erosion has been proven defunct. As transhumant pastoralists move, they dispose of pine conifers and brushwood, mitigating wildfire risk. Migrant livestock depositing excreta upon grazed land boosts soil fertility and facilitates seed dispersal. Carbon sequestration, biodiversity conservation and preservation of cultural and linguistic diversity are additional advantages.

Historically, the connection between transhumant communities and the State has been characterised by mistrust, tension and discord. The Forest Acts of 1865 and 1878 designated forests as safeguarded State assets. Animal grazing, shifting cultivation and collection of forest resources, essential to forest-dwelling groups, were made illegal. After Independence, forest legislation remained rooted in hierarchical management. The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 restricted vast forest tracts under the guise of conservation, hindering livelihoods and causing displacement. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 finally acknowledged these “historical injustices” and recognised forest dwellers’ rights over land and resources.

Mobile pastoralism has been dismissed as archaic by policymakers. Climate plans recognise for­es­try and agriculture but overlook rotational grazing and rangeland transhumance. Education, healthcare and employment opportunities are designed for settled populations. During migration, pastoralists are detached from public utilities, including veterinary care. For women, physical hardships intersect with anxiety, chronic stress, erratic health, language barriers and social stigma.

Seasonal education centres established for Gujjar-Bakkerwals in Kashmir and tribes in North Sikkim are a praiseworthy initiative. Yet Himalayan pastoralists are rarely accepted as stakeholders in land resources. Rehabilitation during the construction of hydel projects or national parks invariably excludes them. Alpine pastures near international borders also face security monitoring, affecting pastoralism.

Some studies show that the local pastoral economy is evolving towards an agri-horticulture-based economy because grazing land is dwindling. The 2025 livestock census recognised the existence of herders and pastoralists. The Centre has urged states with sizeable transhumant populations to assist pastoralists under livestock and animal-husbandry schemes. After centuries, this seasonal drift may finally gain some credibility and subsistence.

editorials.title: A pittance: Editorial on why Rs 200 pension is no social security for India’s elderly
editorials.passage:
The Union government recently defended the monthly pension of Rs 200 for the elderly under the National Social Assistance Programme. To a question from an Opposition member about whether there was any proposal to revise the amount, the minister of state for rural development, Kamlesh Paswan, informed the Lok Sabha that various impact assessments of the NSAP have indicated “satisfactory implementation” and “overall satisfaction” among the beneficiaries, ruling out any plan to revise the amount, which has remained unchanged for 19 years. There can hardly be an argument for keeping the pension frozen given the sharp rise in the cost of living. How can the beneficiaries be satisfied with such a pittance? Moreover, a recent report commissioned by the government itself, conducted by the Delhi-based Academy of Management Studies, found that the Centre’s fixed monthly pension support for elderly citizens, widows, and persons with disabilities has sharply declined in real value over the last decade due to inflation. The monthly sum of Rs 200-500 has effectively lost nearly 45% of its purchasing power.

The inadequacy of this pension becomes starker when set against the steep challenges faced by the aged. A 2024 NITI Aayog report, Senior Care Reforms in India , noted that 78% of the elderly have no pension cover and only 18% have health insurance. A study by FICCI found that senior citizens spend, on average, Rs 8,028 for in-patient care in public facilities and Rs 31,933 in private facilities. Significantly, India is standing at a transformative point in its demographic journey. By 2050, over 300 million Indians will be over 60 years of age, making India a nation with one of the largest senior populations globally: Rs 200, surely, cannot constitute any form of social security. Nor can India’s ageing population be expected to remain indefinitely dependent on government subsidies or family charity. Policymakers must recognise the economic potential of the expanding ‘silver economy’. Data from the World Economic Forum suggest that global consumer spending by the elderly could rise to $34 trillion with one in three dollars being spent by a consumer aged over 60 years. But for India to tap into this segment, policy has to reimagine the elderly as an economically productive segment. The government must also identify those below the poverty line, build an integrated system of inflation-indexed pensions, provide affordable healthcare, insurance and opportunities for dignified work for the elderly.

editorials.title: First step: Editorial on Meta’s $18-billion child safety settlement
editorials.passage:
Meta has reached a landmark settlement in the United States of America, agreeing to pay nearly $18 billion in penalties and make major changes to its platforms. The penalties are for violating child privacy and endangering children with addictive social media platforms. As part of the settlement, Meta has agreed to limit how long teenagers can spend on its platforms, a concession that strikes at the heart of the company’s business model of maximising user engagement to increase advertising revenue. The tech giant’s capitulation is heartening because several studies have pointed out that social media can be like quicksand for youngsters. The Pew Research Center found that about one-third of American teenagers used leading platforms almost constantly, and a former Meta safety engineer reported that 51% of teenage Instagram users surveyed had experienced harm online, with the offending content being removed in merely 0.02% of cases. A study commissioned by Facebook itself revealed that 13.5% of British girls reported their suicidal thoughts intensifying upon using Instagram. The settlement thus rightly holds Meta accountable for products that exposed young users to harm.

Some of the steps that Meta must now take include a default two-hour daily limit for users under 18, silenced notifications during school hours, interruptions in continuous scrolling, strengthening age verification and expanding parental supervision. But these safety features are still rudimentary. Teenagers can still easily circumvent age checks by entering false birth dates, using adults’ credentials and so on. Moreover, targeted advertising, private messaging and several compulsive design features remain largely untouched. Critics have also pointed out that Meta may actually benefit from settling: it avoided an indicting judgment and part of its payment is conditional on TikTok, YouTube and other rivals accepting comparable obligations that will affect their earnings. Even so, the settlement can establish a basic template for firmer global action without restricting youth’s access to useful information and expression. Comprehensive privacy and online-safety legislation targeted towards children — as has been passed in Australia — independent platform audits, transparent risk assessments, strict limits on children’s data collection, digital-literacy programmes and accessible mental-health support are some of the ways in which children can be kept safer online.

editorials.title: Economics and education reform
editorials.passage:
Everyone wants a reform of our education system but, believe me, no one knows what form or forms it should take. Government committees, real experts, self-styled experts, teachers, managers, students, no one, absolutely no one, has any useful idea that can actually change something without damaging something else. Hobby horses, therefore, become prescriptions because there’s no analytical framework to hang it all on.

There is also the homogeneity assumption that education means the same thing to everyone. It doesn’t, because what if I prefer to be uneducated and rich, rather than educated and poor?

The main problem is that education isn’t seen through the lens of economics. Instead, it’s seen as something desirable in itself quite apart from its utility.

Also, no one is able to define education. Is it literacy and numeracy or is it something more? If so, what and how much is that more?

If it’s only literacy and numeracy, what can you actually reform? Given that education is all about value addition to a human, no different from, say, cooking when something raw is converted into something edible, and given further that maximum value addition happens with the ability to read, write and do some basic arithmetic, reform means nothing, absolutely nothing. It’s just a grievance. After all, there’s only one way to teach a person how to read, write and count.

And there lies a very large economic question: if value addition to a human after primary school starts to diminish — and it does — how is the cost-benefit analysis of education to be done?

As is usual in economics, it’s important to look at education as an activity that involves two factors of production, labour and capital. Those who keep talking about reforming education never frame reform like this.

But they need to see that education is both labour and capital intensive. You need lots of both at all levels. And, while labour intensity remains more-or-less constant as you go up the ladder, capital intensity increases.

It’s also an industry characterised by what economics calls ‘constant returns to scale’. This means that if you double or triple or quadruple the number of faculty (labour) and facilities (capital), the output of value added humans will also double or triple or quadruple.

Economics also tells us that because of this feature, the long-run average cost of production remains the same. That makes scaling easier and possible. That’s why it’s so easy to educate hundreds of millions of people quickly.

However, there’s a problem: value addition at each level keeps coming down. In other words, if you expand the output of education, you will spend a lot of money but get less per unit of money spent. I have never heard anyone talk about this aspect.

How can this be, you will ask, when doctors, engineers, scientists, etc are being produced? But think: without the ability to read, write and do sums, you can’t produce doctors, engineers, scientists etc. Value addition is maximum at that lowest level.

So we shouldn’t confuse what is valuable with value-added. The utility derived from a doctor is very high but it’s still not as much as it was when he or she became literate and numerate. It is like going from 0 to 1 and from 1 to 1.7.

Since no one knows what the comparative utilities are, no one also knows where to start. It’s easy to say ‘improve the system’. But what exactly does that mean? More labour or more capital or more of both? And at what level?

This labour-capital problem hasn’t been solved by any country, including the developed ones, at any level. But the more successful ones, in order to keep the capital requirements manageable — largely in Europe — have focused on controlling the supply of students rather than the supply of educational institutions.

Thus, only a small fraction of school leavers, around 20 per cent, are found eligible for college. The rest get skilled. It’s a draconian system but mind you, these are fully democratic countries like Germany, Switzerland, Austria etc. All of them fervently believe in equal opportunities.

There are two other problems. One, the demand for education is a derived demand. It does not exist for its own sake because it involves opportunity costs.

The time spent in learning must eventually translate into a stream of income. Otherwise, it’s a waste of time and money.

Two, there is the capital stock problem. Just as all old machines aren’t capital, all knowledge isn’t capital. Replacement costs money and someone has to decide which stock to replace and with what. This has a direct bearing on syllabus changes.

It’s possible to go on in this vein but suffice it to say the best way to ‘reform’ the education system is to keep its economics at the forefront rather than woolly and ill-defined objectives that work at cross purposes. Or don’t confuse a skill, which is what reading, writing and arithmetic are, with intellectual attainments.

Published on August 31, 2026

editorials.title: Nepal floods: lessons in managing Himalayan rivers
editorials.passage:
The catastrophic floods that struck Nepal’s Rasuwa district and the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 offer a sobering reminder of how rapidly a high-altitude hazard can become a downstream disaster. What unfolded was not simply a conventional rainfall-induced flood, but a complex chain involving the cryosphere, unstable mountain terrain, river blockage and sudden release of stored water. Preliminary assessments indicate that an ice-rock avalanche associated with a glacier collapse in Tibet entered the Lhende Khola, temporarily obstructing the river.

Water accumulated behind the blockage before the natural barrier failed, sending a powerful surge of water, ice, rock and sediment downstream into Nepal’s Bhotekoshi river system. The event destroyed bridges, roads, houses and other infrastructure, causing significant loss of lives and leaving many people missing. The significance of this event extends well beyond Rasuwa. It demonstrates how interconnected Himalayan hazards are becoming — and why conventional flood-risk assessments may no longer adequately capture the risks facing mountain communities and downstream infrastructure.

Himalayan river flows are governed by the interaction of monsoon rainfall, snowmelt, glacier melt and groundwater.

Climate change is altering these components at different rates, increasing uncertainty in the timing and magnitude of runoff. Glacier retreat is particularly important. As ice masses lose volume, meltwater contributions can initially increase before declining as available glacier storage diminishes. Changes in snowfall further modify seasonal runoff.

A glacier or ice-rock collapse can rapidly transform into a river catastrophe when debris blocks a channel and creates a temporary natural reservoir. Failure of that blockage can release water suddenly, carrying enormous quantities of sediment and boulders downstream. Unlike a conventional rainfall flood, such an event may originate far upstream, develop with little warning and occur without intense rainfall at the location where destruction takes place.

The Himalayan risk landscape is increasingly characterised by interacting hazards rather than isolated events. A warming environment can influence glacier stability, snow conditions and high-altitude terrain, while intense precipitation can increase runoff and slope instability.

The resulting chain can be expressed simply: cryospheric change -- ice/rock failure -- river blockage -- temporary storage -- sudden release -- debris-laden flood -- downstream infrastructure failure. The significance lies in the amplification. A localised high-altitude event can become a major disaster far downstream. This calls for a shift from managing “floods”, “landslides” and “glacier hazards” independently towards multi-hazard, basin-scale risk management.

The answer cannot be another isolated infrastructure project. A resilient approach needs to be adopted and this could include:

(i) High-altitude hazard surveillance: Continuous satellite and ground-based monitoring of glaciers, unstable slopes, snow cover and glacial/debris lakes.

(ii) Real-time basin intelligence: Integrating cryospheric, meteorological, seismic and hydrological data into common operational platforms.

(iii) Multi-hazard early warning: Warning systems must detect not only rainfall floods but also GLOFs, ice-rock avalanches, landslide dams and sudden dam-break-type surges.

(iv) Downstream evacuation protocols: Communities in vulnerable river corridors need warnings that translate directly into clear evacuation decisions.

(v) Climate-resilient infrastructure standards: Roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and settlements should be designed using forward-looking hazard assessments rather than historical averages alone.

(vi) Transboundary data cooperation: Himalayan hazards cross borders; early-warning information must do the same.

(vii) Basin-scale risk planning: Flood, drought, hydropower, agriculture, urban water supply and ecosystem management should be considered within the same river-basin framework.

The tragedy in Nepal is a warning about a Himalayan system in transition.

In India, Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries link high-altitude cryospheric changes with densely populated plains, critical infrastructure and major agricultural and economic activity.

India therefore needs to strengthen cryosphere monitoring, real-time hydrological intelligence, multi-hazard early warning and climate-resilient infrastructure planning.

Particular attention should be given to identifying upstream hazards, rather than assessing flood risk only at individual locations. Stronger information-sharing with Himalayan countries would improve lead times and preparedness.

The writer is National President – Ecological & Economic Resilience Council, WICCI

Published on August 31, 2026

editorials.title: The complaint that never retires
editorials.passage: A Friend in Mumbai recently forwarded me a meme: “Gen Z employees need a trigger warning before receiving feedback.” He is a Baby Boomer, and he was chuckling. I didn’t have the heart to remind him that in 2013, TIME magazine put his children’s generation on its cover as “The Me Me Me Generation” — entitled, tech-obsessed, narcissistic. Nor that in the 1970s, when he was young and wore bell-bottoms to Marine Drive, Tom Wolfe had branded his lot the original “Me Generation”, too busy with self-fulfilment to care about society. His own father, no doubt, had opinions about long hair and Kishore Kumar. The prosecution’s charge sheet, it turns out, is a hand-me-down. Every generation inherits it, edits the nouns, and serves it on the next. Newspapers from the early 1900s carried sweeping complaints about idle, pleasure-seeking youth. Gen X were slackers; Millennials were snowflakes, and Gen Z, apparently, are unemployable divas who want to discuss their feelings and leave at 6 pm sharp — a scandal in a country where sitting at your desk till the boss leaves was long considered a core competency. Give it 15 years and Gen Z managers will be complaining that Generation Beta refuses to answer their neural implants after work hours. ALSO READSuccession by scramble Why do we keep doing this? Psychologists call part of it the “kids these days” effect: people judge today’s youth against their own present-day selves, forgetting they were once 23, clueless, and convinced the world owed them an interesting life. Memory is a flattering editor. The uncle who despairs at a Gen Z hire “job-hopping” has quietly deleted the memory of how he switched from the family textile business to a bank, over his own father’s loud objections, because the salary was better and the office had air-conditioning. There’s ego in it too. Admitting the young might be adapting sensibly to a changed world means admitting our expertise has a shelf life. It is more comforting to conclude they are broken than that we are becoming obsolete. And so the Instagram reel becomes proof of narcissism rather than what it mostly is — the response of people handed a camera, an audience, and an algorithm at age 12. But — and here both sides must lean in — the young are not blameless in this pantomime. Every generation arrives convinced it has invented authenticity, burnout, and the critique of hustle culture. A young Bengaluru techie recently explained “quiet quitting” to her father with the solemnity of Newton unveiling gravity. Her father, who spent the 1990s in a PSU perfecting the art of the extended lunch and the strategically placed files, listened with remarkable restraint. ALSO READDon’t mess with markets The truth is that each cohort is a product of its circumstances. The generation that queued for Bajaj scooters and telephone connections chased security because it had seen scarcity. Millennials, mugged by the 2008 crash even as India’s IT dream matured, redefined success as meaning rather than the corner office. Gen Z, raised on precarity, climate anxiety, and a phone that never sleeps, negotiate boundaries because nobody else will do it for them. Traits read as moral failure are usually rational responses to the hand dealt. So, one lesson for each side. Elders: before diagnosing the young, check whether the same complaint was once filed against you. It almost always was — possibly by a grandparent who considered your Maruti 800 an extravagance. Youngsters: the greying colleague across the table survived licence raj, liberalisation, Y2K, and demonetisation. Some of that scar tissue is wisdom, and mining it is cheaper than acquiring your own. The workplace does not need a generational war; it needs a trade agreement. The old have context, the young have current software. Neither travels well alone. And if all else fails, remember the great unifier: every generation believes the one after it cannot draft a proper email — and every generation before it believes the same about them.

editorials.title: I’m giving birth as a battle rages over maternity care in Ireland. We shouldn’t have to pay to feel safe
editorials.passage:
T here were no chandeliers in the public ward where I spent my first days as a mother, at the oldest continuously operating maternity hospital in the world. The room echoed with cries, the well-worn floor bouncing under footsteps, the windows looking out on Dublin’s city centre.

Now the Rotunda hospital, where I’m due to give birth again soon, is counting down to its 1 millionth baby. It is also at the centre of a bitter debate over plans to reform Ireland’s two-tier state healthcare system, so that those who pay to “go private” in public hospitals no longer gain an unfair advantage over those who don’t.

A chandelier is the background for the Rotunda Private’s soft-lit webpage , which lists fees of up to €4,500 to be treated privately in this public hospital. Maternal healthcare in Ireland is provided free by the state, and there are no stand-alone private maternity hospitals in the country. But in the public hospital system, patients who can afford it can pay to access continuity of care with a private consultant, private scans and the right to request a private room after birth.

Ireland is an outlier in Europe by not providing free universal primary healthcare. But at least in public hospitals, its two-tier arrangements could finally be ending. A radical overhaul of the state healthcare system seeks to ensure equal access for every citizen. The “Sláintecare” plan was launched nearly 10 years ago with cross-party support and aims to deliver equal access to health services based on individual patient need, not on ability to pay. But it has still not been fully implemented.

Under the reform, hospital consultants on new public-only contracts are barred from carrying out private work in public hospitals. More than 60% of consultants have signed up to the new contracts in exchange for pay that can exceed €300,000 (with on-call duties and overtime). With no private maternity hospitals, giving birth is finally set to be made entirely public.

But a backlash has exposed both a worryingly low obstetrician-to-patient ratio, and the resistance of these highly paid senior doctors to a fairer, single-tier health system. Ireland has fewer hospital consultants than most countries in the EU, with many medical graduates emigrating . The lowest uptake for the new public-only contracts is in obstetrics and gynaecology, at just over half.

The extent of private activity in Ireland’s public healthcare system and the fight for a single-tier system puts us at the centre of a Europe-wide debate over separating the two.

The government recently prevailed in a long-running standoff with the Rotunda’s management by threatening to cut funding. This followed the revelation that, despite the ban, consultants on public-only contracts were still treating private patients in this public hospital, using public resources, while billing insurers for hundreds of thousands of euros of care, with the Rotunda’s board’s permission.

Allegations that private consultants gave financial gifts as high as €1,500 to public-only colleagues to deliver their private patients’ babies on weekends fuelled the controversy.

Senior figures at the Rotunda have argued that women should be able to choose between public and private. But if there is a shortage of consultants, surely all their time needs to go to higher-risk pregnancies whether the mothers can pay or not?

A Rotunda staff member who sees public and private patients assured me that births take place in the same delivery rooms, and that patients are meant to be seen according to need. “The sickest women often get the best care,” she said. She suggested the dispute was less about maternal “choice” than about a revenue stream that hospitals don’t want to give up. A fully public system was “the only way to have truly equitable care”, she said.

Beyond maternity, there are wider concerns about unfair use of public hospital resources for private healthcare. Despite Ireland being a wealthy country with high spending on health , public hospital corridors are often lined with patients on trolleys, sometimes waiting days for a bed, while children spend years in agony on lists for spinal consults.

Nearly half the Irish population relies on private health insurance, as in many cases this means they can skip the long waiting lists in public hospitals. I have basic health insurance, but I went fully public for maternity care during my first pregnancy, paying for prenatal testing, which I feel should be free.

As a public patient without complications, I was cared for by midwives at the Rotunda. Ireland has low maternal mortality but one of Europe’s highest C-section rates, and midwife-led care can offer less intervention and should be expanded, as the WHO advocates .

Midwives gave me freedom in labour, helped my baby latch, taught me to use a blanket with the smell of my skin to get him to sleep, while I bled in shared toilets and fed myself one-handed. Now, just a few years later, some of the free midwife-led antenatal classes I found crucial are stripped back. And not everyone in Ireland can access midwife-led care. Our government, seemingly championing public care, is also overseeing a crisis in midwifery staffing, driven by state cuts.

Around a quarter of pregnant women in Ireland go private or “semi-private”, an option that the state health service still officially says is available in all maternity units in the country. In practice, however, private maternity care is gradually being eliminated. At the National Maternity hospital, an unprecedented 150 women were turned away for private care in just six weeks in June and July, fuelling a campaign against women losing this “choice”.

But any patient who requires it should be able to see a dedicated consultant obstetrician on a public-only contract. And while many women have traumatic experiences of giving birth in Ireland, surely we should be fighting for every pregnant person to have access to the care they need – not just those who can pay.

A health worker I know opted for private care for her second baby after experiencing missed complications and absent consultants during her first public maternity. But in her work she sees consultants “using the public system to their advantage and funding a lot of their private practice through it.”

Weeks ago, a still-developing body inside my belly flickered on ultrasound. I was told to come back in a month because of a borderline concern. As a public patient, I worried about falling through the gaps.

Since then, a brilliant midwife and public sonographers referred me to consultants including top foetal medicine specialists listed on the Rotunda Private site. I see them for nothing as a public patient. This is how the system is meant to work, escalating care according to need.

Yet it is gutting to know there is a perception that I could be risking my baby’s health by not “going private”, for the continuity of care that paying patients receive and which midwives have been demanding be made standard for all .

I trust the people working hard to provide strong public care, and we shouldn’t have to “go private” to feel safe. If everyone is equally relying on one system, there is real pressure for change.

There is a history in Ireland of bishops, doctors and conservative politicians railing against free healthcare for mothers and children, desperate to maintain control and profit.

I want a fully public, equitable health system. For that to work, those in power must ensure resources and accountability.

My Rotunda maternity ward looked across to a statue of Charles Stewart Parnell, the first president of the Irish National Land League – a mass movement against private monopolies. Ireland’s revolutionary proclamation envisioned “cherishing all the children of the nation equally”. What better way to cherish every child equally from their first breath than a fully public maternity system?

Caelainn Hogan is a journalist and the author of Republic of Shame: How Ireland Punished ‘Fallen Women’ and Their Children

editorials.title: Space junk punched a new hole in the moon. It’s not ours to abuse
editorials.passage:
O n 5 August, a piece of a derelict SpaceX rocket traveling at 5,400 miles an hour met with the moon and punched a fresh hole into it near Einstein Crater . Astronomers were thrilled. The European Southern Observatory caught sodium and lithium flaring in the debris plume and called it a bonus. The media called it a light show. Nobody was physically hurt, so nobody is responsible, and within a week the story was gone.

I have spent 20 years tracking the junk humanity leaves behind in space for a living, and I want to tell you plainly what that crater actually is: a receipt. It’s what you get when an entire industry treats the sky, and now the moon, as a place to dump what it no longer wants, and calls the dumping “normal operations” or “space exploration”.

Here’s my thesis, and I won’t soften it: we don’t own the moon, but we’re behaving as though we did, and that behavior has a name. It’s the oldest colonial instinct there is, dressed up in aerospace engineering. Take what you want, leave what you don’t, and let someone else, or something else, absorb the cost.

Stewardship asks what we owe a place. Ownership asks what we can extract from it before anyone stops us. Right now, in cislunar space, ownership is winning by default, because nobody with power has bothered to claim the alternative, and power doesn’t reside in controlling outcomes but rather in the ability to make choices. Remember this.

So, let’s start with the plain facts of the object itself. The Falcon 9 upper stage that hit the moon launched in 2025 carrying lunar landers, finished its job, and was simply abandoned in a high orbit that happened to cross the moon’s path. Nobody designed a deliberate end for it. The curvature of spacetime and the sun’s radiation pressure did the steering instead, for months, until a predictable, computable trajectory ended predictably, in a fresh scar.

SpaceX didn’t choose to hit the moon. But it did not prevent the collision, which, in an industry with the money and the trajectory software to do otherwise, is likely a choice all the same. That is my first point, and it is not an isolated one. Companies have the power to not allow their rockets to hit the moon. Moreover, rocket bodies have hit the moon before, in 2022 and earlier still, and are always treated as curiosities rather than as pattern.

The pattern is the second point, and it’s where I stop being generous. Look at what we have already done to low Earth orbit, the space closest to home.
