Tens of thousands of tracked fragments, and uncountable smaller ones, now circle the planet because for 60 years, operators launched first and asked about disposal never. Abandonment is not disposal, but those with power have chosen it to be so.

Starlink alone accounts for more active satellites than the rest of the world’s operators combined, and its own operators report rising near misses as the constellation grows. We built that congestion through a very specific kind of confidence (aka hubris): the belief that space is big enough to absorb whatever we throw into it, forever, without a bill ever coming due.

It’s the same hubris a mining company has about a river, or a fleet has about a fishery, right up until the fish are gone. We are simply exporting the same appetite further out, because the moon, unlike the ocean or the atmosphere, has no way to fight back. No air to burn up what we drop on it. No tide to wash away what we leave behind. Whatever debris we send there is, for all practical purposes, permanent. You’ll still find bags of astronaut poop on the lunar surface from the Apollo program.

Which brings me to the third point, the one under all the others: why does this keep happening, when the physics has been understood for decades and the fixes are neither exotic nor expensive?

The honest answer is entitlement. Not carelessness – entitlement. There is a difference between not knowing better and knowing better and doing it anyway because nobody will stop you.

This is the same posture empires have always taken toward frontiers they didn’t build and don’t have to live inside the consequences of. Plant a flag, extract the value, leave the mess for whoever comes next, and call the mess someone else’s problem, or better yet, call it nobody’s problem, because there was never an owner to complain.

That isn’t a metaphor. It’s a fairly literal description of how spacefaring nations and companies currently treat the moon, a place that legally belongs to no one and is treated, in practice, as though it belongs to whoever gets there first with a bigger engine. People love to own the profits without owning the consequences of them left in their wake.

To be sure, I don’t think most of the engineers doing this work are villains, and I don’t think this particular impact was reckless in the way, say, a rocket exploding over the Caribbean and scattering debris over a populated area would be (wink). This piece of debris hit an empty stretch of lunar terrain in daylight, and it genuinely did hand scientists a rare, useful dataset. Some operators are also trying to do better. Companies now design certain missions with deliberate deorbit plans, and there is real, if slow, movement toward international norms for orbital debris mitigation.

I don’t want to pretend none of that exists. But good intentions from a minority don’t change the system’s default setting, and the default setting, according to recent evidence, is still: launch, abandon, hope nothing important gets hit. Isolated best practice is not governance. It is public relations for an industry that still has none.

So no, nobody owns the moon. Under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, no nation can claim it, and no company can either, whatever their marketing suggests about future colonies and mined regolith. But ownership was never really the problem. Nobody owned the lands where Native Americans thrived either. The problem is that we are acting out ownership’s oldest habits, extraction without accounting, expansion without consequence, on a body we all agreed, on paper, to hold in common.

A crater near Einstein Crater is a small thing by itself. What it represents is not small at all.

We have a narrow window left in which the moon still looks the way it has looked for billions of years, before the coming decade’s hundred-plus missions turn “who hit it this time” into a monthly headline instead of a rare one. We can spend that window building the tracking, the disposal rules, and the accountability that stewardship actually requires. Or we can keep doing what we did on 5 August: witness something we built come out of the dark, watch it hit a place we don’t own as if we did, and call it a light show.

Moriba Jah is a professor of aerospace engineering and engineering mechanics at the University of Texas at Austin

editorials.title: The Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us all
editorials.passage:
C limate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.

The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes . The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.

Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI , which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts , water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.

The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.

Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations . Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.

Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India , something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.

This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots , identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.

And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.

Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.

The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Trump’s plan to sell off a part of Yosemite is what oligarchy looks like
editorials.passage:
D o people still say a car was “sold for parts”? Because the US is being sold for parts or just handed over to the oligarchy. It’s a fire sale, a bankruptcy auction, it’s a planned dismantling of everything from its military to its institutions of higher education to its scientific research to its public lands.

And while the threat to sell off part of Yosemite National Park is about a quarter-mile parcel on the park’s edge, Yosemite is a crown jewel in the national park system and, arguably, the world’s first national park.

To let any bit of it be sold off for the benefit of a corporation’s planned development on the park’s western border would compromise the inviolability of national parks and sacrifice public good for the sake of private profit. This is of course the ongoing agenda of the Trump administration .

Public lands belong to all of us, a gift from the past because people worked hard to protect these forests, mountains, canyons, and a trust for the future, because the public should include everyone in this country alive now and everyone yet to come.

The Trump administration’s ruthless efforts to turn over public lands for mining and logging and fossil fuel exploitation while it also dismantles the Forest Service and Park Service is about turning longterm well-being for the many, human and more than human, into short term profit for an elite.

These public lands have many kinds of value – the trees and grasslands are sequestering carbon as part of a natural climate amelioration, the mountains are watersheds, and most of these natural places now are key to rural tourism and outdoor recreation economies.

White people first entered Yosemite valley in the early 1850s, on a military campaign to punish, displace, or exterminate the indigenous people there who were interfering with another era’s environmental destruction: the Gold Rush, whose miners were hunting out the game, cutting down the trees, polluting the rivers, and massacring the region’s original inhabitants.

Some of the early visitors recognized Yosemite’s extraordinary scenic beauty of its oak grasslands, high canyon walls, waterfalls. By the 1860s, photographers such as Carleton Watkins and Eadweard Muybridge had made images of Yosemite that were shown internationally. The place became iconic before many white people had visited it.

In the spring of 1864, Abraham Lincoln signed into law a bill establishing that “Yosemite Valley’s premises shall be held for public use, resort, and recreation; shall be inalienable for all time.” It was originally managed by the state of California, since the federal government had little presence in the west and was busy fighting the civil war.

Yellowstone national park, on the other hand, was set aside eight years later as a federally managed preserve because Wyoming and Montana were not yet states and is usually recognized as the first national park.

The document Ulysses S Grant signed said the place was to be “reserved and withdrawn from settlement, occupancy, or sale under the laws of the United States, and dedicated and set apart as a public park or pleasuring-ground for the benefit and enjoyment of the people.”

There was always a lie in the foundation of Yosemite, Yellowstone, Death Valley, the Grand Canyon and many other parks, in that they were Indigenous peoples’ ancestral homelands long before Columbus set sail or Lewis and Clark headed west.

In Yosemite, those wrongs have been addressed over the past 30 years by changes in signage, representations of the place’s history, and opening to the traditional usage and ceremony of the original inhabitants’ descendants. The flawed premise of national parks matters, but so does the fact that the system kept these places from being privatized, developed and destroyed.

But that is what is now happening to the Park Service as a whole: Trump has been funneling Park Service money meant to be spread across the country to his pet projects at the White House and in Washington DC including gilding statues and the incompetent $16m painting of the reflecting pool.

Michael Scherer reports in the Atlantic that there’s a fast-track approval process for funding Trump projects out of Park Service funds, while the national park service as a whole is being starved. He notes there’s “a decrease of $854m, or 68%, in spending on projects in park regions outside the Washington area in the first eight and a half months of fiscal year 2026, compared with the full prior fiscal year. During that same period, spending around Washington increased by about $100 million.”

The Trump administration proposes to further slash the number of park service employees, who had already been reduced by 24% in 2025.

To give away a piece of land is one form of harm to the parks, to take away the park’s workers, whose labors protect endangered species, waterways, land, prevents fires and provides public services from search and rescue operations to education to clean restrooms is another.

To open up the ancient sacred site of Chaco Canyon in New Mexico to fracking is yet another form of destruction by the Trump administration underway. The same is true of the 90% reduction of the Bears Ears and Escalante in Utah.

As the Associated Press reported earlier this month that this radical shrinkage undoes “protections established by his Democratic predecessors on public lands that are sacred among many Native Americans. Trump administration officials and congressional Republicans have sought to expand drilling, mining and logging on public lands, while removing protections for imperiled species and rolling back rules for conservation.”

Yosemite was first established as protected land during one civil war. Another is underway about whether the federal government exists to serve the good of the many or the profiteering of the few. A small parcel in Yosemite is nevertheless a big indicator of who this country belongs to and whose rights and interests matter.

Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. She is the author of Orwell’s Roses and co-editor with Thelma Young Lutunatabua of the climate anthology Not Too Late: Changing the Climate Story from Despair to Possibility

editorials.title: OnlyFans and AI training: why gen Z doesn’t care where our money comes from
editorials.passage:
B y now, we all know the shape of financial nihilism: the throw-your-money-at-anything reaction to the dissolution of the slow, linear path to wealth; the prediction markets , meme stocks , cryptocurrencies and microluxuries growing in its place. We’re left in an economic no man’s land. But financial nihilism only describes where we put our money. What about how we earn it in the first place?

The modern economy has long relied on our need for stable employment – to pay the mortgage, to keep our kids fed, or, for some, to chase prestige and power – to generate the work ethic that keeps the wheel of production turning. None of this is going well for young people. Our jobs are insecure , we can’t afford houses, we’re deferring having kids (if we have them at all), and only 6% of us say a leadership position is our primary career goal. Hope is one of the economy’s most productive inputs, powering our willingness to endure long hours. When the production function of income – the mechanism that turns hard work into a stable salary, then a mortgage, then a pension – breaks down, so does our relationship with the input. I call this production nihilism: my generation’s growing indifference to the kinds of work we’re willing to participate in, and where we’re willing to earn.

“Normal people are asleep. Good,” a young woman running her craft business at nighttime tells the camera in Shopify’s latest commercial. Partially thanks to all-in-one e-commerce platforms like Shopify, many of us have mastered the art of polyworking. These are jobs our high school career advisers could hardly have imagined – platforms such as Mercor, where white-collar workers train LLMs to do their job; “ YouTube empires ”; the much-covered millions being made by young women on OnlyFans; non-sexualized escorts . Some are supplementary, some are enough to eventually become a primary source of income. Americans seem to be coming around to the idea of “portfolio careers”, with more than half calling them more desirable than traditional careers for a future workforce.

Take away the feasibility of long-term goals and our willingness to wait for “the good life” collapses. So we redirect our motivation to grind and save into channels that pay out sooner – cash, yes, but also autonomy, flexibility or a sense of identity. Fifty-seven percent of gen Z report having a side hustle, well over double the boomer rate. Day jobs start to function as financial anchors, paying the rent while our side gigs do the identity work. After all, “writer” plays far better on a Hinge profile than “analyst”.

With no solid formula for our futures, more of us are experimenting with what it means to interact with the economy at all. The cultural counterpart to this economic logic is a series of attitude shifts to work, nervously cataloged as trends: the gen Z stare , or faked productivity . I recently wrote about the slow death of the prestige career , where – thanks to AI – companies no longer require a robust team of entry-level workers to scale.

We’re living through a transition in our economic relationship with the future. The cultural theorist Lauren Berlant described how an “anticipatory present” kept people bound to an economic system: enduring the short-term in the hope for a promised version of the long-term. Profoundly unable to imagine – let alone attain – a prosperous future, young people may be among the first generations to name this for what it is: foreclosed . When the promise of a future stops working, we “maxx” for the present, extracting value as quickly as possible with whatever assets late-stage capitalism permits us to spend. It’s the other side of the “ little treat ” economy.

Neoliberalism, the system that raised us, offers a convenient way forward: everything can be commodified if we try hard enough. When western society was first learning this lesson, France’s artists gave voice to the unease of their postwar consumer boom. The film-maker Jean-Luc Godard’s Two or Three Things I Know about Her follows Juliette, a Paris housewife, as she prostitutes herself to keep up with the lifestyle being aggressively marketed to her. She decides to sell her afternoons, her time, her body. It’s a precursor, in many ways, to the gig economy of platform capitalism: Juliette optimizes any assets at her disposal to enjoy the present moment.

The New Wave tried to warn us against the relentless tide of commodification. But where Godard and his contemporaries channelled their anxiety through women as objects, gen Z reclaims Juliette’s image – not as a helpless, bored object, but as subject. We are agents of our own relationship with the economy. Less despairing, less passive, less accepting: gen Z’s nihilism feels distinctly active. Production nihilism leans into a new definition of work, forcibly detaching us from the neoliberal “good life” fantasy that’s clearly stopped delivering . Nietzsche described nihilism of this kind as a process of clearing away dead values. Which is what production nihilism does: it detaches us from the neoliberal “good life” fantasy that’s clearly stopped delivering . Refusing to accept the current economic system as the endpoint of our search for meaning, we improvise a new set of values as we go.

But is there real agency here? There’s an idea circulating in Silicon Valley: that “high-agency” individuals – those who think for themselves and act without being told – will be the ones to survive the coming AI disruption . This isn’t really agency. It’s the anticipatory bind Berlant warned us about, another story about how to succeed in an economy where fewer of us will realistically be able to. No wonder we’ve stopped caring about where our income comes from, when its source no longer determines where we end up.

Alice Lassman is an economist who writes The Intimacy Economy, a Substack and forthcoming book on the economics of connection, care and relationships

editorials.title: It is now almost certain the world will warm past 1.5C. But ‘net-negative’ emissions are still possible
editorials.passage:
Anthony Albanese is in Palau this week for the annual Pacific Islands Forum and regional security is expected to top the agenda.

China is testing nuclear-capable missiles in the Pacific, prompting talk of a new regional agreement. The United States-Iran war has exposed a reliance on costly fossil fuels that is undermining Pacific economies.

And as the world comes perilously close to the Paris agreement’s 1.5C temperature goal, a record-breaking El Niño looms in the Pacific Ocean .

But the forum will be missing key leaders – Solomon Islands’ prime minister, Matthew Wale, made a shock departure, flying out of Palau just hours after arriving, in order to deal with a looming leadership challenge back home.

And the Kiribati president, Taneti Maamau, the Samoan prime minister, Laʻauli Leuatea Schmidt, and Vanuatu’s prime minister, Jotham Napat, are also not attending. It is unclear if Fiji’s prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, will be present.

Pacific nations will want Albanese to address the world’s key security threat – climate change. As president of negotiations of the Cop31 climate talks in November, Australia can work with the Pacific to keep 1.5C within reach and secure much-needed finance for island nations at the climate frontline.

Since the second world war, the United States has maintained fortified bases in the Pacific and an unrivalled deep-water navy (the US also regularly tests long-range missiles in the region ). However, China’s investment in military capabilities has challenged the status quo.

In July, China launched a nuclear-capable test missile that flew over multiple Pacific nations and hit waters close to Tuvalu’s exclusive economic zone .

This sparked calls for a new regional security agreement: Wale said China’s missile test was “not the act of a friend” .

Ironically, it was Solomon Islands that signed a security deal with China in 2022. This changed the security dynamics of a region long aligned with the US and Australia (notwithstanding concerns about nuclear testing and decolonisation).

Since then, Canberra has pursued a web of bilateral deals to shore up Australia’s place as Pacific security partner – first with Tuvalu (2023) , then Naoero (formerly Nauru) (2024) , Papua New Guinea (2025) and Vanuatu (2026) . Discussions are ongoing with Tonga and Solomon Islands. The most recent agreement, an Ocean of Peace Alliance signed with Fiji in July, is a mutual defence pact that is open to other Pacific nations to join.

Canberra was already pursuing a treaty allowing for coordinated regional responses to disasters and other crises . China’s missile test may have opened the door for something more.

The Middle East conflict has pushed the Pacific toward an energy crisis. About 80% of the region’s energy relies on imported oil products , much of which would normally transit the strait of Hormuz. Even before the US-Iran war, Pacific island countries spent an eye-watering percentage of GDP (between 10% and 25%) buying fossil fuels to run power plants, generators, boats and vehicles. This compares with a regional average of 8% spent on education and 6% on health .

The Middle East conflict has only added to the bill. According to a new report , Fiji’s annual refined fuel import costs could rise by US$375m (A$520m) if high oil prices persist. This is more than Fiji’s entire healthcare budget.

Renewable energy offers a clear solution. Replacing diesel generators with grid-scale solar and battery storage could save Pacific countries about US$700m (A$520m) each year in avoided fuel costs .

The incoming chair of the Pacific Islands Forum, the Palau president, Surangel Whipps Jr, wants the region to become the first in the world 100% powered by renewables . He says investment of US$120m (A$ 166m) is needed for Palau to add 60MW of solar and battery storage , which would enable 90% of its power needs to be met by renewables.

When climate change was first debated at the UN Security Council in 2007, Pacific countries argued the impacts of a warming planet were “no less serious than those faced by nations and peoples threatened by guns and bombs”.

Since then, Pacific Islands Forum leaders have explicitly reaffirmed climate change is “the single greatest threat” to Pacific security.

In 2025, Earth was 1.44C warmer than the long-term average. Pacific countries are reeling from stronger cyclones, dying reefs and ocean acidification. Without urgent action to shift away from coal, oil and gas impacts will get much worse. Just this week, the world’s oceans are the warmest on record , fuelled by climate change and a rapidly intensifying El Niño event.

It is now almost certain the world will warm past 1.5C. Yet it remains possible, following a temporary “overshoot” , that countries can limit warming to 1.5C by the end of the century. This will require deep and immediate emissions reductions and some carbon dioxide removal to achieve “net-negative” emissions .

Limiting global warming to 1.5C is a line in the sand for low-lying Pacific nations – “1.5 to stay alive” is the slogan. Pacific negotiators helped secure this temperature goal in the 2015 Paris agreement.

Pacific nations expect Australia to reaffirm global commitment to 1.5C. Australia is helping Fiji and Tuvalu host a pre-Cop summit in October that will remind world leaders the survival of island nations is at stake.

Pacific countries will also seek new finance for a Pacific-owned climate fund to invest in community-scale adaptation projects.

Some argue collaboration with the Pacific in the lead-up to Cop31 is an expensive exercise . But climate action is crucial to Australian strategy in the region. Investing in renewables and adaptation in the Pacific is an investment in shared security, even as geopolitical competition sharpens between China and the US.

Wesley Morgan is a research associate at the Institute for Climate Risk and Response, UNSW. This article was originally published in the Conversation

editorials.title: More and more undergrads are living at home. That’s a crying shame – here’s why
editorials.passage:
I f the headlines are to be believed, no one should want to be a student in England any more. And yet this September and October, a record number of school leavers will begin their journey at university, unwilling to let rising costs, a regressive loan system and dimming graduate job prospects blot out the promise of the best years of their lives. The burden now placed on today’s students has grown so heavy, though, that it is reshaping people’s experience of higher education: new data from the university admissions service Ucas shows a marked rise in the number of students planning to live at home with their parents , rather than moving away to study.

It’s first worth stressing that this new arrangement is not, for the most part, a voluntary one. That’s clear in the gap between those “choosing” to stay at home and those who have no choice at all: among students from England’s poorest neighbourhoods, more than half now expect to live at home while studying, compared with just under a fifth from the least-deprived areas.

The student rental market is the main culprit – it is now forcing many teenagers to fork out more than £10,000 a year just for basic accommodation, even in cities outside London. Since the liberalisation of housing regulations in the 1980s (alongside an influx of wealthy international students), private landlords have been given free rein to jack up prices while housing standards worsen, with damp, rat-infested accommodation now becoming a normalised part of the student experience . A recent study by the National Union of Students found that an appalling 84% of students reported significant issues with their housing , with almost half living with mould, despite the extortionate costs many are now paying. It’s no surprise, then, that many of my peers feel they have no option but to stay at home.

This may seem like an easy solution, but it, too, comes with its personal costs. A lack of personal space as well as family conflict can mean worsening mental health for some students who stay at home. Many will also inevitably miss out on the life skills a person only learns when living independently. Then there’s also the very real risk of being excluded from the cultural and social highs of university life – the joys that make it worth persevering through gruelling deadlines and exam schedules. That trade-off is evident in those around me who have already made the reluctant retreat to study from home: all have struggled with isolation, and some have dropped out of university entirely. With graduate prospects collapsing, it’s the lifelong friendships built on campuses and in student accommodation that count more than ever in the university experience. Take that away and replace it with an hour-long commute from your childhood bedroom, and you begin to wonder if any part of getting a degree is really worth it.

Meanwhile, students on difficult terms with their parents are left in an impossible position, forced to cough up eye-watering sums simply to maintain a healthy distance from them. In this respect, particularly for those who have experienced restrictive upbringings, the freedom to explore adult life at university remains an invaluable part of discovering our real selves. Crippling costs therefore make what should be the most liberating chapter of our lives so far instead feel like trading one set of restrictions for another.

It has always been fashionable for older generations to bemoan the laziness of “today’s youth”. Yet how can anyone expect a generation to properly grow up while being denied the hallmarks of adult life? Stuck under a parent’s roof at university, and denied the economic mobility that comes with a graduate job once they leave, my generation is being condemned to live out its own twisted Peter Pan fairytale.

Luckily, it’s not all doom and despair. The recent Renters’ Rights Act has provided much needed breathing room for students , shifting the needle back in favour of tenants over Britain’s landlords for the first time in decades. Certainly, the ability to cut our tenancy short has been a gamechanger over the summer; previously, we had to keep paying rent for rooms we couldn’t stay in. But students will need more than just tweaks to their current arrangements; we need rent controls, a shift out of the private rental market, and investment into affordable, purpose-built complexes designed for university life.

There is one silver lining to all this: earlier this year the UK’s biggest student landlord warned that profits could slide because of lower room occupancy, which could be exacerbated as students choose to study from home, so the tower of cards is looking awfully close to coming crashing down. Perhaps if this model has finally run out of road, then students’ housing needs can finally be released from the grip of profiteers .

Rohan Sathyamoorthy is a writer from south-west London

editorials.title: The hill I will die on: No self-respecting adult should use the term ‘picky bits’
editorials.passage:
I t’s a bittersweet time of year. The season of tiny shorts is giving way to wondering whether the trousers you last wore in May still fit. I’ve already seen Christmas tat in The Works; only Sainsbury’s winter-spiced bleach is the greater festive harbinger of mortality. At least we’ve hopefully seen the end of the heatwaves. And, with it, the scourge of the phrase “picky bits”.

For the blissfully uninitiated, picky bits is apparently the new national name for spending £8 on three trays of pastry-wrapped “exotic” confections in a tragic facsimile of the delicious, high-quality deli items our European neighbours enjoy every day of their goddamn lives. Every summer, the ranges get more off their nuts: who knew your picnic needed Turkish grilled pepperoncini and dressed salsa verde chickpeas? (It doesn’t.)

Before brands such as M&S, Waitrose and the Co-op leapt on the cutesy phrase as a way of bankrupting you for sticks of cheese wrapped in ham (and loads of plastic), picky bits had more innocent origins as one of the many terms that Britons use for slapping tomatoes, coleslaw and crisps on the table and letting everyone choose their own dinner.

Its potentially infinite variety demands almost as many names. Back when Twitter was fun, discussions of regional – or just family – difference like this knocked hours off British productivity levels. You call it a picky tea? Table dinner? Lovely. My friend’s mum calls it, quite wonderfully, “a cold collation”. Mine calls it “salad”, despite the sad bistro leaves (served in bag, obviously) being the last thing anyone wants, compared to the salami and dips. Salad cream, however, is crucial. I love linguistic quirks such as this. You call a roll a breadcake, a barm, a cob? Delightful!

That is, until brands get on board. Suddenly, endearing domestic chatter becomes mortifying when shouted from a 4ft-tall poster at the train station. Removed from the context of the family’s novelty salt and pepper shakers and a sibling squabble over the last sausage roll, picky bits feels – as the New York Times once wrote in a canonical 1994 report about Mr Blobby – like “a metaphor for a nation gone soft in the head”.

Every time I see the phrase in public life it makes me want to do civil disobedience. It’s the Boaty McBoatface of dinner time, exposing our once-repressed nation’s surprisingly twee core and total disregard for shame. Sure, my own personal lexicon is full of embarrassing nonsense, but you’re never going to see [REDACTED] on a billboard overhanging the A4.

Also, most of these supermarket picky bits taste incredibly underwhelming. Have some self-respect and tear a rotisserie chicken apart with your bare hands next time you go to the park.

Laura Snapes is the Guardian’s deputy music editor

editorials.title: After the flash flood disaster, here is what Nepal really needs
editorials.passage:
Five days after the flood that struck the Rasuwa and Nuwakot regions of Nepal, the number of missing people is growing. The whereabouts of more than 4,700 people are unknown, while local authorities are struggling to cope with the shocking number of recovered bodies.

This disaster hit home for me. My husband’s village was wiped out, his relatives narrowly escaping the flood.

For more than seven years, I have worked in climate advocacy. I have sat in policy meetings, written reports on glacial risk and spoken at panels about the particular vulnerability of Himalayan communities.

I thought I understood what was at stake. I was wrong. The horror and despair I have seen in affected communities are hard to describe.

What is worse is that the threat is far from over. Preliminary scientific evidence indicates that a massive ice-and-rock collapse in the high Himalayas triggered a cascading event in the Lhende Khola, sending a sudden surge of water, rock and sediment into the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli river system.

As a result of this movement, a lake has formed near the Nepal-Tibet border and may yet cause a second flood.

While Nepal could not realistically have prevented the initial collapse, the scale of the disaster highlights glaring gaps in disaster risk reduction and preparedness under a changed climate reality.

The country urgently needs real, funded investment in early-warning systems for glacial and flood hazards in high-risk mountain corridors. Right now, authorities must urgently map and monitor unstable glaciers, landslide-dammed lakes and river corridors, while restoring damaged sensors and establishing 24/7 real-time communication among mountain monitoring stations and downstream communities.

We need much stronger upstream hazard monitoring and river-corridor planning, including transboundary data-sharing with China, risk-sensitive infrastructure planning and continuous assessment of unstable glaciers, slopes and temporary debris dams.

Clear evacuation triggers, emergency shelters and multiple warning channels, including SMS alerts, sirens and local radio, must be activated immediately to give people enough time to move to safety as the threat of secondary flooding escalates.

Here in the Himalayas, the warming of the region is destabilising our cryosphere: our glaciers, our glacial lakes and our mountain slopes. With each year of record heat that passes, the risk of exactly this kind of catastrophe rises.

Therefore, beyond the early warning systems, we also need climate-resilient infrastructure, as well as locally led adaptation and disaster preparedness designed with and by the people who actually live with the risk. There must be meaningful investment in vulnerable communities, especially those downstream.

We need bridges, roads, hydropower and public facilities that can withstand floods, landslides and other cascading mountain hazards. We need locally led adaptation to encompass resilient public services, communications systems, livelihood protection and recovery support so that vulnerable downstream communities have the resources they need even before disaster strikes.

Nepal cannot do all this alone. Wealthy nations, which are the biggest emitters of greenhouse gases and thus most responsible for the present climate crisis, should not limit their response to repatriating their dead citizens from my country and issuing symbolic gestures of support.

They must now ensure that we have the finance we need to recover and rebuild from this loss, as well as withstand what is to come.

Climate funds should be delivered now, not as future pledges. Nepal should be able to draw from the Loss and Damage Fund so that direct and timely assistance can reach families, and homes, livelihoods and infrastructure can be rebuilt. It must be new money, not aid re-labelled, and must come as grants, not loans. It must be easy and fast to access, not buried in a bureaucratic process and a timeline set by the next climate summit.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Yet we are among the most climate-vulnerable nations on earth, where warming doesn’t arrive gradually but as a wall of water and mud tearing through a valley in minutes.

We are not asking for charity. We are demanding climate justice: to be compensated for suffering from a crisis we played almost no role in creating.

Being compensated for this disaster does not mean the Nepalese people will be just passive recipients of foreign funds. Nepalese society has already mobilised to help fellow citizens struck by the disaster.

The response of young people in particular has been quick and unequivocal. Across Nepal, the youth have organised a Rasuwa Relief Group, mobilising resources, coordinating support and sharing verified information.

As I write this, an army of youth is signing up to volunteer for relief and rescue operations on the ground. It is a powerful reminder that young people are not only among the most vulnerable to climate change. We are also its first responders. We are leaders in moments of crisis, even when no one asked us to be.

Seven years ago, I showed up to my first meeting of young climate activists, unsure if anyone would listen. Watching this generation mobilise in real time, faster and more effectively than most institutional responses, tells me the work of the past years has not been in vain.

If there is one lesson I want people to take from what happened to Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, it is this: climate action cannot stop at mitigation targets and policy conferences, in rooms where conversations are slow and meandering like lazy rivers.

When our leaders sit down to decide what happens next, the youth and the most affected, vulnerable communities must be given a seat at the table. Perhaps listening to their voices can save us from the next disaster.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: The looming failure of Operation Economic Outcast
editorials.passage:
Last week, Pakistan announced that it will not comply with the latest sanctions the United States imposed on Iran and will continue trading with its neighbour. The news came just days after China made a similar statement.

The sanctions announced by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on August 24 under “Operation Economic Outcast “ are supposed to be “the toughest sanctions in history” designed to impose “the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world”.

Earlier, President Donald Trump called it in a social media post “ECONOMIC D-DAY.” He promised “tremendous economic consequences” for any nation that extended Iran “any type of lifeline”.

Six months of US bombing and naval blockade have produced no US victory, so the plan now is to starve Iran into capitulation. The new approach is illegal, cruel and will fail for several reasons.

To begin with, there is the historical record. Economic sanctions do not bring down governments determined to survive them. Yes, sanctions can impoverish populations, empower the security services that control smuggling and hand the targeted nation a rallying point built on US malice. But they do not topple governments.

Consider, as well, the basic arithmetic of the world oil market. Bessent proposes to remove Iranian oil exports from a world that has already lost a fifth of its oil supply because the Strait of Hormuz is shut. The US proposes to deepen a stagflationary shock already being borne by Europe, Japan, and its other allies, and orders those countries to enforce sanctions that will throttle their economies.

Above all, the campaign is targeted against China, which buys more than 80 percent of Iran’s oil exports. If the US sanction the Bank of China or the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Beijing will not respond with a mild diplomatic note. It will restrict its rare earth exports, because it has already run this experiment once and won.

In April 2025, China imposed export licensing on heavy rare earths in response to Trump’s tarrifs and within weeks American and European automakers were idling assembly lines for want of rare-earth magnets. In October 2025, China announced a far more sweeping package and Washington folded, agreeing to pull back its own newly expanded restrictions on Chinese companies in exchange for a suspension of Beijing’s measures for a period of one year.

The April controls have never been lifted and the suspension of the October measures ends in November. So Bessent has chosen this moment, just over two months before China’s expanded rare earth regime returns and weeks before Chinese leader Xi Jinping is due for a visit in Washington, to inform Beijing that it is either with the US or against it. This is a trap for the US of its own making.

Beijing has made its position clear. “China has made clear on many occasions its firm opposition to illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council. Economic warfare and maximum pressure provide no solution,” Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Lin Jian told journalists.

It is not just the opinion of the Chinese government that the US sanctions are illicit. Article 2(4) of the UN Charter prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. The US repudiation of the UN Charter goes far beyond Iran.

Of all 193 UN member states, America is now the country least aligned with UN-based multilateralism. In January 2026, Washington withdrew from more than 60 international organisations. In 2025, it voted with the international majority in just five percent of recorded UNGA resolutions.

At this point, every government should draw three conclusions. First, the US has repudiated the UN Charter. Second, American security assurances are unreliable. Third, relying on dollar-based trade leaves states vulnerable to US sanctions.

Around the world, countries are turning to new defence arrangements, such as the Mecca Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan. They are also predictably moving away from settlements in US dollars and reducing their holdings of US treasury debt in their foreign reserves. They are also turning to China’s open-weight AI models to meet AI needs instead of paying for American proprietary models.

Thucydides’ ancient account of the Peloponnesian War is being read in our day as a mirror of the US–China rivalry. Its most famous line is the taunt Athenian generals gave to the people of Melos in 416 BC, that “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” Yet just a dozen years after the Athenian generals made their taunts, it was Athens that was defeated by Sparta.

The US now taunts Iran and other countries in the same tone. Pride goeth before the fall and no government today is more arrogant than the US under Trump and his enforcer Bessent.

Governments around the world will not follow the US blindly into disaster.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: Why Tamil Nadu’s factories are death traps for migrant workers
editorials.passage:
A t around 10.40 am on June 21, the female migrant workers’ quarters at a seafood processing plant in Tamil Nadu’s Tiruvallur district, was almost full. Many of the women were still sleeping because it was a Sunday, their day off.

The quarters were situated on the first floor of the plant, operated by St Peter and Paul’s Sea Food and Exports. The floor was also crammed with equipment, including refrigeration machinery, pipeline systems and an ice flakes generator machine.

Suddenly, the occupants began to feel breathless. Ammonia, a poisonous gas, was leaking up from faulty infrastructure in the plant below, and quietly filling up the room.

When news of the gas leak broke out, Kiran Kumar immediately rushed to the hospital where victims were being taken. Kumar is a social worker with Jesuits Migrant Services, which aids and advocates for the rights of migrant workers.

He was keen to help the workers and their families in any way he could. But at the hospital, authorities denied him permission to meet the workers. Kumar was unsurprised – this was an obstacle he often faced in his work.

Over the next few days, Packiaraj SJ, a Jesuit priest and the head of the organisation, and Kumar, called government officials, and police and hospital administrators, seeking permission to enter the hospitals where victims were admitted. They did not acquiesce. Kumar tried visiting the hospitals directly, but police stationed outside turned him away, saying that his services were not needed.

Kumar pleaded with authorities, explaining that he could be useful to them. In his decade of work with migrants, Kumar had gained fluency in Hindi. He had also become familiar with villages, districts and cities in states like Odisha, Jharkhand, Bihar, Assam and Uttar Pradesh, from where most workers to the state migrated. He had even picked up other local languages and educated himself about communities that lived in these regions.

It was only a full week after the incident that Kumar was allowed to meet the women – by then, 18 had died. According to the bail order of one of the company’s directors, which Scroll accessed, most of the deceased women had been brought to the company by the same contractor named Suresh. Four were minors. Nearly 70 workers had been hospitalised, many of whom remained in a coma for several days.

Authorities contacted Kumar because they had been unable to trace the family of a deceased worker for three days. The information on the worker’s Aadhaar card was inaccurate, leaving them with no way to find the name of her village or members of her family.

In the days and weeks that followed, Kumar helped coordinate the tracking and return of many other injured workers.

Most of the deceased were Adivasis. Fourteen were from Odisha’s Keonjhar district, and belonged to the Juang community, categorised as a particularly vulnerable tribal group. There were also others from Adivasi communities in Assam and Jharkhand. The high number of Adivasi victims led the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes to take note of the incident, and write to the district collector, seeking details about it.

Even a month or so after the incident, Kumar recounted, when he went to see a patient who was in a coma, police stopped him. “Sometimes, I lose my temper when things like this happen,” he said. “But I’ve also become accustomed to this attitude from officials.”

Kumar and other activists told Scroll that the June incident was only the most recent evidence of the immense vulnerability of migrant workers in Tamil Nadu, which is among India’s most industrialised states. Migrant workers are crucial for this industrialisation – while the state government is currently conducting a survey to determine the number of such workers in the state, according to the 2011 census, 34.87 lakh people had migrated to the state for employment.

In most such incidents involving deaths and injuries of these workers, a crucial factor is that companies typically house the workers within factory sites – often in dehumanising conditions that expose them to major health risks. Even when factories and plants provide housing to workers outside worksites, the accommodations usually violate building codes, are overcrowded and pose safety risks.

Further, their freedoms are typically restricted. A 2024 report of the Corporate Accountability Lab, which examined seafood processing plants in Andhra Pradesh, underlined this concern, noting that migrant workers were at high risk of forced labour. This was particularly so among “those whose housing is tied to their employment, a common practice across the supply chain”, it stated.

This type of living arrangement is not limited to seafood processing plants, or Andhra Pradesh. Scroll ’s investigation across industrial areas in Chennai and Tiruvallur revealed that workers in a wide range of sectors, including automobile, general engineering and chemical manufacturing, as well as in smaller enterprises like restaurants, textile stores and petrol bunks, live in the premises of their workplaces, or adjacent to them.

Activists regularly deal with cases in which workers are injured or killed, or go missing. In June, for instance, a worker at a Larsen & Toubro site in Chennai died, and 48 were injured, after a corroded staircase collapsed in the workers’ labour camp in Nandambakkam. In September 2025, another worker, from another Larsen & Toubro site in Kattupalli died after tripping on a staircase in a makeshift shelter near the site. Around 100 employees were lathi-charged by police when they protested after the incident, demanding that the worker’s family be paid compensation for the death.

Scroll contacted all the companies named in this story, as well as the Tamil Nadu government, seeking responses to arguments that they had not adequately protected migrant workers. This story will be updated if they respond.

“Most incidents don’t come to light because the employers quietly take care of it, pay for treatment and send them home with a small amount,” Kumar said. He added that employers have nearly complete control over migrant workers’ lives. “What we are seeing with migrant labour today is a new urbanised form of bonded labour and enslavement,” he said.

This story is part of Common Ground , our in-depth and investigative reporting project. Sign up here to get the stories in your inbox soon after they are published.

T he isolation of workers at the Tiruvallur seafood unit was evident when Scroll visited it in early July – even villagers who lived next to the plant said they did not know that so many women were living within the premises. “We would see some of the women sometimes, many of them looked 15-16 years old,” said Selva, a neighbour. “They would walk to the small shop down the road.”

On the day of the leak, when locals rushed to help, and carried the women outside one by one, they were surprised.

There was a similar lack of transparency at other industrial sites Scroll visited . Conversations with workers in the area around another seafood processing unit in Chintadripet, in Chennai, revealed that the unit housed migrant workers. But the security guard at the gate dodged questions about them – it was only when another local overheard our conversation and emphasised that workers lived inside that the security guard hesitantly agreed.

But a senior staffer I met, who was walking into the premises, paused for a few seconds when I asked about migrant workers, then denied outright that any were employed at the unit, let alone that they lived inside.

Owners of seafood processing units, many of which process shrimp, often housed workers on site, explained Siddharth Chakravarty, a researcher with the National Federation of Small Scale Fishworkers. Workers, including those from Adivasi communities, “are usually made to stay inside the compounds, similar to the plant in Tamil Nadu, often in premises adjacent to processing facilities”, he said. “As a result, when ammonia leaks occur, which is common, they cause severe impacts on health and at times deaths of workers.”

Sara Abraham, a former lawyer and sociologist, explained that in fact, according to section 16 of the Interstate Migrant Workmen Act, 1979, employers are required to “provide and maintain suitable residential accommodation to such workmen during the period of their employment”.

But, she noted, “There is no clarity about the type of accommodation, where it should be. The company can claim that its barracks are temporary accommodation, though workers live there for years on end”. Further, the law “doesn’t make it mandatory for the accommodation to conform to standard building codes”, she added.

The lack of clear guidelines ends up disadvantaging workers, Abraham said.

“When employers provide workers with substandard housing, which is furthermore confined to being within a compound with security at the gate, workers have little leeway to demand better accommodation, or rental expenses,” she said.

Indeed, a 2026 study on workers in Chengalpattu in Tamil Nadu found that 59.6% had makeshift housing, and that 32.77% felt their living space was unsafe. The study also found that 61.2% of the workers suffered from poor mental health.

The practice of housing workers on site was also common in an area of Tiruvallur called Kosapur, which Scroll visited, and which has a high concentration of industries, including wood and engineering industries. “Nobody lives outside, they all live within the factory,” said a shopkeeper.

Most workers hesitate to speak to outsiders, especially those from civil society organisations or the media. One worker, from Uttar Pradesh, said in a brief conversation that the facilities for them were not good, but that he did not have any objections. From the outside, the accommodation building that was visible looked dilapidated – several men were waiting their turn for a shower in an open-air bathroom.

Conversations with workers were easier at an event for migrant workers held in Chennai in late July, organised by the Jesuits Migrant Services. Here too, some of the workers appeared to have accepted the difficulties they lived with.

Among them were four young men, aged between 19 and 21, from Assam. They worked and lived within the compound of a factory in Chennai that manufactured vehicle parts. The men said that they did not mind staying at the factory and that they only wished that there were more toilets and bathrooms. “We are about 13 people in a room, so it would help to have extra toilets,” he said.

But when asked more questions about safety on the site, workers tended to remember adverse incidents.

Similarly, after some thought, the young men from Assam recounted that a colleague had lost a toe while operating a machine. “The employers paid his hospital bill and gave the family Rs 2 lakh and sent him back,” one said.

Two other young men from Odisha at the Chennai event had worked for two years in a factory in the city that manufactured tractor components, and where workers stayed on the first floor. “If we stay outside, a lot of time goes in travelling, so staying inside is fine with us,” one said. He noted that the rooms were large, and that the sleeping arrangements were not crowded because workers alternated between day and night shifts.

The manufacturing processes at the unit required high temperatures, which workers said affected the living quarters as well. The problem was exacerbated by the fact that workers also had to use the rooms to cook their meals. “Yes, it does get very hot in the rooms,” the worker said.

A fter the June incident, both the directors of the seafood export company were accused of offences that included culpable homicide and using child labour.

In their bail application, the directors of the company said that the company had an annual turnover of Rs 300 crore and that they were “willing” to pay Rs 10 lakh per victim. They also claimed that the incident was an “accident” and not a case of negligence.

The accused were released on conditional bail after paying a bond of Rs 25,000 and were asked to compensate the families of the deceased workers, and those who were injured.

But Kumar and other activists said that securing compensation was often an uphill task because companies did not usually formally register workers. Activists explained that avoiding registering their workers also gave companies the freedom to pay lower wages and demand longer working hours.

The Tamil Nadu government has an online portal that allows workers to self-register. But Kumar said it was unrealistic to expect workers to learn about this process and see it through.

The consequences of the lack of transparency are grave. Kumar and other activists said if the seafood plant workers had been registered properly, authorities would have been more quickly able to determine how many people had died or been injured, and trace their families.

But instead of following a systematic process, Abraham said, after the incident, workers were immediately shifted into a wedding hall, where they stayed for the next few days, and where media and social welfare groups were not allowed to meet them. She argued that such an approach, which the government often resorted to in such situations, “creates a bizarre situation of workers moving into a deeper situation of confinement after a major tragedy which has already completely upended their lives”.

In mid July, Scroll met the families of two of the ammonia leak victims who were still undergoing treatment at the Rajiv Gandhi Government Hospital in Chennai. One of them had emerged from a coma just a few days earlier, almost a month after the incident.

The father of one of the victims, from Odisha, said that nobody from the company had called him to inform him about his daughter’s condition. “When I heard about the ammonia leak, I had a feeling my daughter may have been working in the same plant,” he said. He learnt it was her when he received a call from his son-in-law, who worked in the same plant.

The husband of the other victim said he was furious that the company had not reached out to them. “An agent from the neighbouring village told my wife about the job, I told her not to join but she insisted,” he said. Since then, the agent had not called “to find out about my wife”, he said.

This was a common situation, Kumar noted. “Many agents bring the workers to the factories and then become incommunicado to family members,” he said. “If they want any help after that, they have no one to call.”

Activists said that companies usually stonewalled their efforts to gather information to help workers and their families.

Kumar is currently working on a case of a death of a worker from Jharkhand. “When we went to enquire at the police station, the representative of the company he worked in refused to disclose the name of the company,” he said. “And when we tried to speak to his colleagues, they blocked our access.”

Construction workers, who were often housed in makeshift accommodations close to their worksites, were particularly vulnerable, he observed. “If something falls on them, or if they fall off a height, nobody is going to know,” he said. “Nobody is held accountable.”

Kumar said many migrant workers in the state were from very remote regions with little exposure to the outside world. This made it imperative, he said, for the government to pay greater attention to how they are brought into the state and placed in the care of the employers.

Packiaraj echoed Kumar’s observations. “It is very difficult to coordinate with the labour department when it comes to migrant worker issues,” he said.

D espite their hardships, many workers Scroll spoke to said that they were glad to have work. “If we were home, we would not be earning so much,” said Asha, a worker from Jharkhand at a copper recycling unit in the industrial town of Gummidipoondi, in Tiruvallur. “This land is feeding us, so we must not complain.”

The town, which is home to many industries, as well as a State Industries Promotion Corporation of Tamil Nadu industrial park, has seen so many migrant workers arrive that a tiny village of sorts inside it is occupied entirely by migrant workers and their families. Though some of the plants in the industrial park provide free accommodation to workers in rooms adjacent to their compounds, many choose to live in the settlement because they have families.

Elderly men in traditional North Indian style dhotis and turbans sat under a tree – fathers of those working in the estate. Even the clinic nearby had its name and other details written in Hindi.

The day before I visited the settlement, a boiler explosion had killed one worker and injured five others at a copper recycling unit at the estate. “We don’t know how many died or how many were injured,” one worker said. “The news we get is never accurate.”

Asha, who asked to be identified by a pseudonym because she was fearful of retaliation from her employers, worked at the same factory. The day I met her, Asha along with two of her colleagues, Anandi and Priya, also identified by pseudonyms, had gone to work in the morning at 8 am, as they usually did. But they were sent back because the plant was shut down after the explosion. “Now that means we don’t get paid for the day,” Asha said.

I asked if they felt that was unfair. “Yes, there are things that happen that are unfair, but how can we complain? We are not in our homes,” she said. “We are in pardes,” a foreign land.

The women then went on to list other problems they faced. They explained that due to the hazardous nature of their work, they are required to wear protective shoes, gloves, glasses and masks. The costs of the shoes and gloves are cut from the workers’ salaries, they said. “They give us the masks for free, but we have to pay for the other things,” Anandi said.

Anandi took out a small bar of soap from her pocket. “Our whole bodies get covered in soot, especially our hands. So we carry soap to wash our hands before lunch,” she said.

Anandi frequently falls ill. “The doctor told me that my chest is filled with soot,” she said. When the workers fall sick the supervisors give them a tablet called Embulide, a painkiller. “When I complained, they told me, laughing, to eat banana and jaggery, and said I would be fine,” Anandi said. When workers are injured or fall ill, they are taken to the hospital, but the bills are left for them to pay, she observed.

If the workers arrive a few minutes late, the security guard slams the gates shut, Asha said. “We have to walk 30 minutes to the factory and we have to walk past isolated wild areas with snakes, and where often drunk men stand and harass us,” she said. “So sometimes we get late, but they refuse to let us in, forcing us to lose the day’s wages.”

Anandi explained that they were paid around Rs 400 for eight hours of work – Tamil Nadu’s minimum daily wage is around Rs 550. “Some money is also deducted,” she said. “Each time, we get a different amount.” The workers from Odisha at the tractor manufacturing company had also complained that they were only being paid between Rs 12,000 and Rs 14,000 a month, or under Rs 500 a day.

Perhaps what upsets the workers the most is that they feel they are treated poorly compared to their Tamil counterparts.

She added, “The Tamil workers can take breaks also, but we can’t.”

Kumar reiterated this observation, noting that migrant workers were also often paid lower wages. “They make migrant workers work overtime also but don’t compensate them,” he said.

“It is much easier to exploit migrant workers than Tamil workers,” he added. “The local workers are aware of their rights and demand fair salary, and also appropriate working conditions.”

At the seafood plant in Tiruvallur, too, villagers living in the area said that locals would only take up general cleaning jobs in the factory. “Some people sweep and clean the outside, but inside, only migrants work,” one villager said. “Our people will not work in such hazardous conditions.”

The seafood plant was shut down after the June incident – villagers said they were relieved, and that they had been demanding its closure for years. But some argued that the move came too late, partly because there was an overall lack of empathy for migrant workers. If locals had died, Selva argued, many “would have gone to the streets and raised a hue and cry. But because they were migrant workers, nobody did anything.”

editorials.title: How Japan’s victory in the 1907 war against Russia strengthened India’s resolve for freedom
editorials.passage:
In 1907, two years after the conclusion of the Russo-Japanese War, the Indian anticolonial leader Aurobindo Ghose drew attention to the geopolitical connections between India and Asia that rendered the political freedom of India from British rule an essential precondition of Asiatic freedom as a whole.

We believe that … the Time-Spirit is at work to bring about a mighty movement … that movement is the resurgence of Asia, and that the resurgence of India is not only a necessary part of the larger movement but its central need. … The position of India makes her the key of Asia. … Her freedom is necessary to the unity of Asia. Geographically, she occupies an impregnable position of strength commanding the East of Asia as well as the West, from which as from a secure fortress, she can strike the nations of the Persian or the Chinese world. Such a position held by a European Power means a perpetual menace to the safety of Asia. It will therefore be the first great enterprise of a Chino-Japanese alliance to eject the English from India, and hold her in the interests of Asiatic freedom and Asiatic unity.

In stark contrast to civilisational Asianists who had emphasised the cultural unity of India and Asia, Ghose highlights here the geopolitical alliances between India and other major Asian countries. The language Ghose uses is one of military strikes, geographical strength, secure fortresses, and strategic alliances that must be formed between Asian countries to “eject” the British from India and thereby ensure the freedom of Asia itself from European empires.

Electrified by Japan’s victory in the Russo-Japanese War of 1905, Indian anticolonial revolutionaries began to organise and prepare for a war against the British Empire. Since India, unlike Japan, was not an independent country, her anticolonial war would have to take the form of a national revolt, much like the one fought in 1857. In the aftermath of the suppression of the revolt, the discourse of war as a path to military and political sovereignty had gone underground and existed furtively within secret societies. Indian intellectuals constructed a discourse of India’s civilisational sovereignty in its place, which emphasised the cultural unity of India with Asian countries like Japan.

Japan’s triumph rekindled the smouldering memory of 1857 and turned it into a revolutionary fire. The military-political route to sovereignty that had been closed by the defeat of the Revolt of 1857 was opened once again, and in the discursive horizon revealed by this new geopolitical imagination, the primary questions were: How had India lost its political and military sovereignty? And through what military strategies, manoeuvres, and alliances could that sovereignty be recovered? In this discourse, the colonisation of India was not attributed to civilizational weaknesses; it was seen as a geopolitical event that could only be ended by geopolitical means, including military and political strategies and alliances that would result in the empire’s violent end.

This chapter explores the origins and nature of a geopolitical discourse of Asianism in India in the wake of the 1905 Russo-Japanese War. It looks at both national and transnational efforts made by Indian geopolitical Asianists to start an anticolonial revolution in India on the one hand, and to form alliances with other Asian and European powers who would help India achieve national sovereignty on the other. It also examines the contradictions and continuities between the discourse of geopolitical Asianism and the discourse of civilisational Asianism that found a new voice in Rabindranath Tagore in the years following the Russo-Japanese War.

In many ways, the birth of Indian nationalism in the twentieth century was the direct product of the Russo–Japanese War. The news of the defeat of imperial Russia by Japan in the war sent a wave of exhilaration through Indians, who envisioned their own future freedom from the British Empire in the image of a free Japan. Thus, it was Japan’s victory, an event that occurred outside the territorial boundaries of India, that inspired the rise of the discourse and practice of Indian nationalism, an extraordinary fact whose significance has been completely overlooked by historians. Also, what was distinctive about this nationalism was that in being connected at its birth with a discourse of Asianism, it was inspired by, and derivative of, a vision of the freedom of Asia as a whole.

Moreover, Japan’s victory demonstrated for Indian writers not her unique military capabilities as a nation but “Asiatic values” and Asian military abilities that had been denigrated for over a century by the British discourse of the civilising mission. Newspapers like Deshbhakti emphasised that “Japan’s admirable qualities … are peculiarly Asiatic … fearlessness of death, … abstinence and self-control, tenderness and humanity,” in contrast to Western nations that were characterised by “aggressiveness, greed, and disregard for other people’s rights in the name of progress.” At the same time, they argued, Japan’s military successes had overturned a key claim of British discourse that Asians were weak and incapable of leading organised campaigns on the battlefield. The Kesari , for example, asserted that the Japanese victory at the Battle of Mukden proved the military capabilities of “Asiatics” as a whole.

There was never any question about the personal courage and endurance of Asiatic troops. But they were told that they were deficient in leadership and organisation and could not therefore hope for victory without being led on the battlefield by European generals. The Asiatics have given an effective reply to this allegation on the battlefield of Mukden. Russia, which occupies the foremost position among the European nations, has been completely worsted by Japan. … It is impossible yet to estimate fully the consequences of the victory of Mukden. It has undoubtedly served to bring the sun of Asia’s glory on the horizon, and there are signs that it will gradually rise to the meridian and spread its refulgent rays far and wide throughout Asia.

Thus, in a single stroke, Japan’s triumph brought the importance of warfare, battles, resistance, and struggle against imperialism to the forefront of Indian public discourse. Editorials expounded on the transformative impact that this demonstration of the military capabilities of Asians had on Indian consciousness. An editorial in the Bengalee, for example, asserted: “We feel that we are not the same people as we were before the Japanese successes. … For the first time in modern history Asia has triumphed over Europe and has vindicated its equality in the knowledge of those arts which have their cradle in Europe.”

Japan’s victory also proved for many writers that mighty European military empires that seemed invincible could be defeated. And if imperial Russia could be defeated, the same fate, they felt, could befall the British Empire. A writer in Kal asserted that “Japan, by her brilliant achievement, has produced the conviction in the breast of every Asiatic that all European Powers are bound to crumble before an energetic onslaught. … The Russo-Japanese War has taught men how intrinsically weak large Empires are and how vastly powerful small states might be.” Echoing the same sentiment, a writer in the Kesari stated, “Japan has shown that an Asiatic power can more than hold its own against a European rival. …”

Significantly, newspaper writers saw in Japan’s victory a sign of the future freedom of India. Because of historical relations between the two “Asiatic” countries, they asserted, “the magnificent qualities which the Japanese have exhibited in the epoch-making war” were ones that Indians also possessed. It was natural, then, for Indians to feel joy at Japan’s success. In the words of a writer for the Kesari: “Japan is today winning the same distinction which India won in olden times. As both India and Japan have been instrumental in raising the prestige of Asia, it is but natural that they should be proud of each other. The new victory gained by Japan in capturing Port Arthur has spread joy throughout India.”

If Indians were to win freedom from the British Empire, these writers argued, they would have to emulate Japan. What distinguished the Japanese was that they were united as a people, whereas Indians were not, they contended. The most important task, then, was to build a sense of unity among all Indians. A writer in Hind Vijaya observed, “Japan owes her victories entirely to the unity prevailing among her people. Indians, if they desire to bring about the rise of their country, should meditate upon and take a lesson from the example set by Japan.” An observer writing for the Spectator for his audience in England noted the constant emphasis in Indian newspapers on the need to emulate Japan as “the first example of a wholly Asiatic defeating a Western Power.

In pointing to the moral of the Japanese victories [native] newspapers continually proclaim a parallel between Japan and the various provinces of India. Japan, they say, rose suddenly from obscurity, entirely through the development of a national sentiment. Only let the people of India unite, let them foster the growth of a national sentiment, and no man can say where they will stop.

The popular reactions of Indians to Japan’s victory in the war were summed up by the same observer in the Spectator: “In India, the native feeling is practically universally in favour of Japan. Everywhere it is apparent, from the larger towns with their native prints down to the small townships of the mofussil, where the daily news is read with eagerness. Articles laudatory of Japan constantly appear. … Native feeling in India is enthusiastically pro-Japanese.” CF Andrews, a close friend of Gandhi and Tagore, endorsed this view. Even in remote villages, he found that the men “talked over the victories of Japan as they sat in their circles and passed around the huqqa at night.”

Indians demonstrated their pride at Japan’s victory and their support of the Japanese cause in several tangible ways.
