A Japanese Widows and Orphans Fund was set up to which “India … contributed nearly a lakh of rupees,” wrote the Gujarati. In addition, an Indo-Japanese Association was formed to “promote friendly relations between India and Japan, and to make literary, religious, educational and industrial investigations.” When news of the fall of Port Arthur reached India, a writer in the Shri Fattesingh Gazette wrote: “In recognition of this brilliant achievement of Japan, some of our townsmen … [gave] expression to their feeling of joy by distributing sweets.”

Excerpted with permission from Asianism and the Fall of Empire: India’s Road to Freedom, Mithi Mukherjee, HarperCollins India.

editorials.title: ‘Fake claims’: Great Nicobar lighthouse project study lists species found in Africa, Amazon
editorials.passage:
Species primarily found in Africa and the Amazon have been listed in a recent environment impact assessment study claiming that they live on Great Nicobar Island.

The report released in April was prepared by WAPCOS Limited, a Gurgaon-based public sector undertaking as part of a proposal to repair the lighthouse and construct tourist facilities at Indira Point, the southern-most point of the island – and of India.

Tables in the environment impact assessment report list tiger fish ( Hydrocynus vittatus ), a native of African freshwater rivers, and the flagtail ( Semaprochilodus insignis), an Amazonian freshwater fish.

Also listed are sambar ( Cervus unicolor ) and barking deer ( Muntiacus muntjak ), two species of mammals found primarily on India’s mainland.

More than 90% of the species listed in the tables in the study have never been reported from Great Nicobar. In many cases the closest sites are thousands of kilometres away.

Ecologists and marine biologists who have spent decades studying Great Nicobar said the report was “shocking” and alleged that it was “completely fabricated”.

The study includes the Eurasian woodcock ( Scolopax rusticola ), a bird of temperate and subarctic Eurasia that is found in Sri Lanka and along India’s western coast only in the non-breeding season, and the Mayabandar rice frog ( Microhyla chakrapanii) , which has only ever been reported from the Andaman Islands but not the Nicobar.

At the same time, the report omits creatures such as the sea turtle, which is prominently found around Indira Point.

Email messages seeking clarifications about this have been sent to Dharamveer Shrivastava, Director, Lighthouses and Lightships, Port Blair, and Aman Chopra, the co-ordinator and a key author of the environmental impact assessment report prepared by WAPCOS.

This article will be updated if they respond.

The report was prepared in the context of the Rs 250 crore Indira Point project proposed by the Directorate of Lighthouses and Lightships, Port Blair, to repair and reinforce the island’s lighthouse.

The project will also include constructing eco-tourism facilities, a convention centre, cafeteria, viewing tower, cycle tracks, a museum as well as a memorial.

Indira Point is located about 5 km south of Galathea Bay, the site of a proposed Rs 50,000-crore transshipment port on the ecologically sensitive Great Nicobar island.

The port is the centrepiece of a Rs 90,000-mega infrastructure project that has been in the eye of a storm. Experts have noted that it will cause enormous environmental destruction and will displace members of the vulnerable Shompen indigenous group. They have also pointed to flaws in the scientific reports that were presented to win approvals.

In June, the lighthouse project proposal was sent to the Andaman and Nicobar Coastal Zone Management Authority seeking coastal regulation zone clearance. The application had a host of supporting documents. They included a detailed project report from May 2025 prepared by the Department of Ocean Engineering of the Indian Institute of Madras, Chennai, and a coastal regulation zone map prepared by Anna University.

Among the documents was the April 2026 rapid environmental impact assessment report by WAPCOS.

The environment impact assessment report has five tables of species reportedly found at the project site – one each for mammals (12 species listed) , birds (29 species), reptiles (11 species), amphibians (seven species) and ichthyofauna (fishes;19 species).

The list of birds is illustrative. Great Nicobar is an internationally acknowledged Important Bird Area with more than 100 species of birds, according to a comprehensive study on the island published by the Zoological Survey of India in 2022. Many of the species found are endemic, suggesting they are not found anywhere else on the planet.

“It is shocking that this bird list has only 29 names,” said Asad Rahmani, former director of Bombay Natural History Society, and one of India’s foremost ornithologists. However, it includes species such as the Hume’s hawk-owl, the Eurasian woodcock and the mangrove whistler “that have never been reported from Great Nicobar”, he said.

The same is true of the tables with mammal and reptile species.

Of the 12 mammals in the table, only three are found on Great Nicobar. How the sambar got listed is a complete mystery.

The case of reptiles is equally intriguing. The 2022 study by the Zoological Survey of India lists more than 30 reptile species from Great Nicobar. But the environmental impact assessment report lists none of these, including prominent large creatures such as sea turtles that are regularly reported around Indira Point.

Of the 11 reptiles in the table, only one – the sunbeam snake – has ever been found in Great Nicobar.

“All this data is highly erroneous,” said an ecologist who has worked in Great Nicobar for many years but did not want to be identified. “Many sections of this report and these tables in particular are highly objectionable or outright shocking.”

Vardhan Patankar, a senior marine biologist with intimate knowledge of the coastal and marine systems of the Nicobars, contended that the environmental impact assessment report “is full of copy-paste material, and that too is not from an authentic source”.

Said Patankar: “The fish list here reads more like an aquarium shop catalogue. Many are simply not found here. To claim these are part of the coastal or marine environment surrounding Indira Point is completely fabricated.”

The Indira Point environmental impact assessment report is only the latest in a string of problematic reports and interventions by leading scientific and research institutions that support the projects proposed on Great Nicobar Island.

Among the earliest was the Wildlife Institute of India, which played a key role in the environmental and wildlife clearances granted to the mega project on the island. The institute was eventually granted projects worth nearly Rs 400 crore to study the biodiversity of Great Nicobar, raising concerns about a conflict of interest.

Then there was the disappearance of coral reefs on the official maps of Great Nicobar Island, as reported by Scroll in October 2025.

The Chennai-based National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management, an agency under the environment ministry, produced maps in 2023 with no coral reefs in Galathea Bay.

This was in stark contrast to the centre’s own maps of 2021 and other scientific studies that reported at least 20,000 vibrant coral colonies. Experts suggested that the maps had been manipulated to facilitate port construction there.

In December 2019, a WAPCOS tender document titled “Traffic Study For Creating Transshipment Port At South Bay, Great Nicobar Island Of A&N Islands” had sought to justify constructing the port in Galathea Bay, another name for South Bay.

The reasoning offered in the report was that “the topography of the island [Great Nicobar] is the best suited [for the port], which has not been damaged much even by Tsunami on 26.11.2004”.

This too flies in the face of evidence. The coastline of Great Nicobar and the entire Nicobar group of islands experienced a subsidence of nearly 15 feet in the immediate aftermath of the earthquake of December 2004 that also caused one of the biggest tsunamis in recorded history.

In fact, the Indira Point lighthouse needs repairs and strengthening because of this subsidence. Before December 26, 2004, it was surrounded by coastal forests, way above the high-tide line. It now stands in the sea.

The irony of this reality appears completely lost on WAPCOS that has prepared the EIA report with “incorrect data”, noted the researcher who did not want to be identified.

Pankaj Sekhsaria was jointly awarded the Prem Bhatia Award for Excellence in Environmental Journalism 2026 for his research and reporting on the Great Nicobar infrastructure project. He has written and edited seven books on the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, including two edited volumes on the Great Nicobar project.

editorials.title: India has an ‘image problem’? Sadanand Dhume should take a closer look at America first
editorials.passage:
It never ceases to amuse me when columnists based in the United States, which has Donald J Trump as its president, offer solemn sermons to other countries on their ‘image problem’. Okay then.

Sadanand Dhume’s brand of clickbait ‘journalism’ is nothing if not clever. His blinkered takes, featuring narratives airier than old wives’ tales, are designed to provoke a visceral response. And his favourite subjects are poor Indians — given that he is the ‘South Asia expert’ at an American think tank — and also because, I suspect, outrage is our national pastime. The best way to get some eyeballs and clicks on social media is to act as an agent provocateur to rile up Indians, an art good old Dhume has perfected over the years.

That said, I shall not summarily dismiss the thrust of Dhume’s Wall Street Journal column, where he writes about India’s ‘global image problem’. There is a grain of truth to what Dhume says about India’s “dysfunctional urbanization”, even though his premise — that American ‘unfavourability’ towards India ought to be our national concern — is patently absurd.

There’s no point denying that “mounds of garbage” or “half-drowned buses on flooded roads” are a persistent problem in Indian cities. But Dhume’s bad-faith argument overlooks the challenges that a country of 1.4 billion people faces and the grunt work that is being done to address these chronic issues.
I’ll spare you the rhetoric and deal with data to show why Dhume’s views are ill-informed, and why his larger narrative is a load of bunk. On the question of civic apathy, where India clearly has some work to do, there is a documented correlation between a nation’s economic prosperity and the strength of its civic sense, individual accountability, and care for public assets.

This correlation, at one level, is driven by behavioural economics and a societal version of Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs.

When a population is trapped in poverty, systemic inefficiency, or a daily struggle for basic resources, the ‘scarcity mindset’ takes over. When cognition is consumed by immediate survival and personal welfare, shared public assets such as parks, trains, or streets are often viewed as objects to be exploited for personal gain rather than as a shared inheritance to be protected.

As a country develops and basic economic security is guaranteed, however, citizens gain the urge to care about abstract concepts such as environmental sustainability, community aesthetics, and the preservation of public goods. So, the correct question is not whether instances of public squalor reflect ‘national character’ (that’s a specious framing), but whether the political leadership is addressing the core problems to create the conditions under which civic sense can flourish.

Even a passing familiarity with India ought to have made it clear to anyone who is interested — let alone a so-called ‘South Asia expert’ — that India is changing rapidly for the better through a concerted push for accelerated infrastructure creation across transport, housing, water, energy, logistics, and digital networks.
As India Matrix points out in an excellent essay on Substack ‘How much of India’s infrastructure was built after 2014?’, “the last 12 years demonstrate, with a precision that data rarely offers a columnist” a story “told in kilometres, gigawatts and crore rupees…”

To illustrate the point, India Matrix starts with freight, where a decade ago India’s rail system lacked dedicated routes for moving cargo. Goods trains competed for capacity with passenger services on the same congested lines. That constraint is now being dismantled. India has built 2,843 km of Dedicated Freight Corridors, linking Gujarat’s ports with the coal-producing regions of eastern India through purpose-built, high-capacity freight infrastructure. Rail transport now costs about Rs 1.96 per km, compared with around Rs 3.78 per km by road.

Similarly, citing the essay, in 2014, barely one-fifth of India’s broad-gauge network was electrified, leaving most trains dependent on imported diesel and exposing railway operating costs to fluctuations in global oil prices. By 2026, electrification has extended across almost the entire network. The electrified route length has expanded at a pace of network transformation greater than what Indian Railways achieved over the preceding nine decades combined. Do take a look at this stunning graphic.

Not just freight: public capex on infrastructure has surged more than six-fold, rising from Rs 2 lakh crore in fiscal 2014-15 to Rs 12.2 lakh crore in fiscal 2026-27. This is indicative of a strategic shift from fragmented execution to integrated planning through mega-initiatives such as PM GatiShakti, Bharatmala, and the National Logistics Policy.

Let me now cite details from the government’s own data available in the public domain.

India now possesses the world’s second-largest road network at 63.73 lakh km. The national highway network has expanded by 61 per cent, growing from 91,287 km in 2014 to 1,46,572 km by March 2026, while four-lane and above highways have more than doubled from 18,371 km to 45,516 km.

In terms of rural connectivity, 99.6 per cent of eligible rural habitations are now connected and over 4.11 lakh km of rural roads were completed between 2014 and 2026, with the budgetary allocation jumping from Rs 386 crore to Rs 19,000 crore.
The number of operational airports has more than doubled from 74 in 2014 to 165 in 2026. Contactless facial recognition through tech integration (Digi Yatra) is now operational at 38 airports, serving over 9.3 crore passengers.

India now operates the world’s third-largest metro network, spanning 26 cities (up from five in 2014), with daily ridership surging from 28 lakh to over 1.15 crore passengers. Route length has quadrupled from 248 km in 2014 to over 1,155 km in 2026. The pace of construction accelerated from 0.68 km/month to nearly 6 km/month.

Over the past 12 years, infrastructure in India hasn’t just grown; the pace of its execution has multiplied, transitioning the country into a highly connected, modern economy with a heavy emphasis on indigenous technology (Vande Bharat, Kavach, Digi Yatra) and integrated logistics.

These are not just statistics but verified data on painstaking nation-building that is accelerating India’s growth by slashing logistics costs, formalising the economy, and driving productivity gains across all major sectors. And this is just one part of the story.

Over the past 12 years, India has undergone an immense transformation in its approach to governance, infrastructure, and poverty alleviation. Before 2014, a significant portion of the Indian population lacked access to fundamental necessities such as safe sanitation, piped water, reliable electricity, and formal banking. The government’s shift from a fragmented, incremental approach to a ‘universal saturation’ model has altered the socioeconomic landscape.

Before 2014, rural sanitation coverage languished at just 39 per cent, with widespread open defecation causing severe public health crises and disproportionately affecting women’s safety and dignity. Sanitation coverage reached 100 per cent by 2019, making India Open Defecation Free (ODF). Over 12 crore individual household latrines were built. Under Phase II, over 83 per cent of villages (more than 4.89 lakh) have now achieved ‘ODF Plus Model’ status, complete with solid and liquid waste management systems.

Piped drinking water through the Jal Jeevan Mission gave 15.8 crore rural households access to clean drinking water through direct connections. This is a jump from 16.7 per cent of rural households with tap water access in 2019 to 81.6 per cent in 2026, drastically reducing waterborne diseases and saving millions of hours spent fetching water.

Thousands of villages were off the grid before 2014, and rural households received a daily average of only 12.5 hours of power. India has now achieved near-100 per cent village electrification. Around 99.6 per cent of eligible rural habitations are now connected by all-weather roads, linking remote farmers directly to markets.
In his vibe-based column, it may have been superfluous for the Wall Street Journal columnist to mention the transformative impact of the Narendra Modi government’s welfare delivery system through the JAM trinity. Before Modi came to power at the Centre, half the country was outside the banking network. As of August 2026, over 59.09 crore zero-balance bank accounts have been opened, pulling in over Rs 3.17 lakh crore in deposits. By linking Jan Dhan accounts to beneficiaries’ biometric Aadhaar identities and mobile numbers, the government has created a direct, transparent pipeline to the citizen.

The saturation of basic amenities and the plugging of financial leakages have served as a springboard for massive upward economic mobility. According to the World Bank’s 2025 Poverty and Equity Brief, India has conquered extreme poverty. The proportion of Indians living in extreme poverty (under $2.15 a day) plummeted from 16.2 per cent in 2011-12 to just 2.3 per cent in 2022-23, lifting roughly 171 million people out of extreme poverty.

Multidimensional poverty — which tracks deprivations in health, education, and standard of living — dropped from 53.8 per cent (2005-06) to just 15.5 per cent (2022-23).

As the poorest citizens moved out of poverty, the middle class swelled. According to a 2025 survey by PRICE (People Research on India’s Consumer Economy), India’s middle class (households earning between Rs 6 lakh and Rs 36 lakh annually) has expanded to over 560 million people across 126 million households.

This demographic now forms the bedrock of India’s domestic consumption story. Spared the daily struggle for basic survival, families are increasingly investing in education, healthcare, consumer goods and digital services.

When a family stops losing workdays to waterborne diseases (tap water and toilets), stops relying on kerosene lamps (grid electricity), and receives welfare without paying bribes (Aadhaar-linked direct benefit transfers), its economic productivity multiplies. This bottom-up empowerment has transformed India from a fragile economy into a resilient, consumption-driven engine, laying the foundation for a developed and economically empowered nation.

The rapid expansion of the Indian middle class is creating a massive demographic of formal stakeholders in the system. As more citizens move into the formal economy, gain access to credit for small businesses and invest in property, their relationship with the state changes. This demographic is driving civic responsibility. The intense debate in the Indian social media space over civic sense, public cleanliness and individual accountability is reflective of this shift.

Dhume’s concern is touching, but he should rest assured that we are taking rapid strides in the right direction. Since he makes such a huge song and dance about New Delhi’s ‘falling favourability’ in Washington, it may be worth pointing out the slight issue with America’s ‘global image’, which seems to be taking a rather sound beating.

Since Dhume places so much store by Pew Research, let me quote from a survey by the same agency. A 36-country survey published in June 2026 finds declining ratings for the United States amid “rising concerns about its foreign policy and the health of its democracy”. Since “global image” is under discussion, Pew Research says “the share of the public who considers the US a reliable partner has declined steeply in many countries since we last asked this question in 2022”.

Across the 36 countries surveyed, a median of 37 per cent of respondents express a favourable view of the US, while 57 per cent have an unfavourable view. In Europe and the Asia-Pacific region, opinions are largely negative: 7 in 10 or more in many of these nations rate the US unfavourably, Pew Research finds.

The agency further adds that “in many of the countries we have surveyed since 2002 — including Canada, France, Germany, Italy, the Philippines, South Africa, South Korea and the UK — positive ratings are at or near the lowest they’ve been.”
It isn’t just one agency. NIRA Data, released in May 2026, commissioned by the Alliance of Democracies and conducted in 85 countries worldwide between March and April 2026, documented “how steeply the United States is losing its global appeal in recent years”. The results, published in The Diplomat, indicate that whereas just “three years ago, the US enjoyed a comfortable lead globally in terms of soft power”, that situation has changed to such an extent that “most countries around the world now view China more favourably than the United States”.
If India has a ‘public squalor’ problem that, according to Dhume, is affecting its ‘global image’, America under Trump has a racism problem.

Stephen Miller, who serves a central role in shaping Trump’s domestic and immigration policies, has increasingly utilised language that emphasises demographic purity and ancestral claims to the country. As The Economist observes, “Senior Trump aides such as Stephen Miller stop only a few inches short of overt racism, talking of ‘heritage Americans’, who are somehow more American than newer arrivals, and ‘remigration’, a buzzword on the nativist right for sending people from alien cultures home… The administration blocked all new immigrant visas for citizens of 75 non-rich countries. Thus, if an American marries a Nigerian, they cannot live together in America, a curb on American liberty with echoes of a darker past.”

Between racism and civic apathy (which India is striving hard to fix), one wonders which one is more morally onerous and has a far more deleterious impact on a country’s “global image”. Maybe we should ask Dhume?

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Mohan Bhagwat’s unity pitch exposes America’s cancel club
editorials.passage:
It is rare for both sides of an ideological divide to be unhappy — even outraged — by the same event and, more importantly, by the message emerging from it. Yet, that is precisely what happened after Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat addressed an event at Madison Square Garden in New York on Saturday.

Let’s consider Bhagwat’s words first: “If you want to call yourself Hindu, you must believe that all paths are leading to the same (goal). And every human has dignity. There is no difference between human beings.” He went further: “If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslim in Bharat, he will not remain Hindu.”
To be fair to Bhagwat, it was a mature articulation of the Indian civilisational perspective, while simultaneously providing an effective rebuttal to those who had opposed the RSS chief’s presence in the United States. More significantly, it offered a striking contrast to the US cancel club, which is liberal in vocabulary but increasingly marked by the instincts of exclusion and cancellation.

Incidentally, a section of the Indian Right is unhappy too, though for the opposite reason. It regards the RSS chief as too conciliatory towards hostile strains of Islamism and Leftism. But that criticism misses the occasion. Bhagwat was speaking at an event devoted to interfaith dialogue. For him to launch into an examination of competing religious doctrines, or the differences between exclusivist Abrahamic traditions and Sanatana traditions, would have defeated the purpose. The event was about multi-faith dialogue. To attend a gathering intended to promote religious harmony and dwell primarily on religious conflict would have been a self-goal.
More importantly, Bhagwat articulated the essence of Sanatana Dharma: diversity, dialogue and mutual respect — not merely tolerance. There is an important distinction between respect, accommodation and tolerance. The Sanatana tradition aspires to respect different paths. Modern secularism generally seeks to tolerate them. Exclusivist interpretations of Abrahamic faiths, by contrast, have historically struggled with the proposition that radically different religious paths can possess equal validity.

Bhagwat appeared to have a larger objective: to use an iconic global platform to take Sanatana Dharma’s message of “oneness in different paths” to an international audience. Placed alongside the politics of the American cancel club, the contrast is stark: universal oneness versus selective liberalism; respect for diversity versus cancellation; integration versus confrontation.

Let’s take the case of the current poster boy of American cancel culture, Zohran Mamdani, who had publicly opposed the RSS event in New York, describing its ideology as representing an “exclusionary vision”. Yet, the irony is difficult to miss. A politics that seeks to exclude a speaker because it considers his worldview exclusionary risks reproducing the very instinct it claims to oppose. Moreover, Mamdani, who objected to Bhagwat’s presence, has had no difficulty meeting Imam Siraj Wahhaj, who has publicly expressed opposition to homosexuality and was named as an “unindicted co-conspirator” in connection with the 1993 World Trade Center bombing case. While Mamdani accuses the RSS, and its current leader, Mohan Bhagwat, of “violently” promoting a “supremacist ideology”, he has described Wahhaj as “one of the nation’s foremost Muslim leaders”.

Herein lies a central contradiction in contemporary ‘liberal’ politics, especially in the West. It advertises pluralism as a cardinal virtue but applies it selectively. Tolerance is readily — and almost exclusively — extended to groups and ideologies regarded as allies; ideological opponents are subjected to demands for exclusion, delegitimisation or cancellation.

Bhagwat’s statement also raises a host of other, harder questions: would similar declarations of theological pluralism be expected from leaders of other religious or ideological organisations? Would Christian or Islamic religious leaders affirm that other religious paths possess equal legitimacy? Would they respect the Bhagavad Gita in the same spirit in which they regard their own sacred texts? Would they affirm that multiple religions can lead to God, truth or salvation?

Not necessarily. And that is precisely where the asymmetry becomes difficult to ignore: the RSS and Bhagwat are frequently treated as uniquely suspect, irrespective of what they actually say, while those on the other side of the religio-ideological divide are treated with kid gloves. This suggests that the issue is not merely the RSS or Bhagwat. It points to a deeper discomfort with Bharat and its civilisational conception of itself.

Bharat often finds itself being cancelled by these very ‘liberals’ and the institutions they control. It is publicly called names, and its civilisational and democratic credentials delegitimised. The annual United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) report is a case in point, routinely attempting to delegitimise the democratic credentials of Bharat, invariably clubbing it with communist China, Islamist Pakistan and autocratic North Korea.

The fact of the matter is that the idea of Bharat is rooted in a civilisation that has, over centuries, absorbed and accommodated extraordinary socio-religious diversity. It offered refuge to persecuted communities, including Parsis and Jews, who were able not merely to preserve their identities but to flourish within the Indic civilisational ecosystem. Jain and Buddhist traditions likewise developed distinctive identities while remaining deeply embedded in the broader Indic world.

These examples complicate simplistic attempts to understand Bharat’s minority issue solely through the Islamic prism. Muslims, of course, constitute a religious minority in the constitutional and demographic sense. But their enormous numbers, internal diversity, long history and profound influence on the subcontinent make the Indian experience very different from the conventional Western image of a tiny minority living precariously alongside an overwhelmingly homogeneous majority. Communities such as Parsis and Jews, Jains and Buddhists offer a more realistic perspective from which to analyse Bharat’s record of civilisational pluralism.

Bharat finds itself in a unique situation where even its supposed allies in the West tend to stand opposed to it, largely because of their innate Christian upbringing, which manifests itself in their outlook despite their outwardly atheistic worldview. Richard Dawkins is a case in point. He fights religious fundamentalism unapologetically. But his lack of understanding of the Sanatana tradition makes him equate it with the Abrahamic faiths he opposes.

A few years ago, Dawkins attacked “Modi’s BJP” as “a tragic affront to India’s secular beginnings”. He described Hinduism as “at least as ridiculous as Islam” and accused contemporary India of betraying the ideals associated with Nehru and Gandhi. Interestingly, he passed this sweeping verdict on “Modi’s India” and “Hinduism” on the basis of an editorial in Nature magazine, which claimed that the Periodic Table and Charles Darwin’s Theory of Evolution had been dropped from the school curriculum in Bharat. As it turned out, it was yet another case of fake news, for the topics had not been removed but merely shifted from Class X to Class XI. The verdict, however, had already been delivered: Hinduism itself was “ridiculous”.

Dawkins is a self-proclaimed atheist, but his cultural assumptions occasionally make him behave like a ‘born-again’ Christian. He criticises PM Modi for foregrounding Hindu identity, yet has described Barack Obama as effectively atheist despite the latter’s very public Christianity. As Micklethwait and Wooldridge observe in God Is Back, “one reason why Barack Obama beat Hillary Clinton was that he succeeded in out-Godding her”. Obama himself writes in The Audacity of Hope: “Kneeling beneath that cross on the South Side of Chicago, I felt God’s spirit beckoning me. I submitted myself to His will, and dedicated myself to discovering His truth.”

If this is the case with the likes of Dawkins, the general intellectual milieu in the West is largely anti-Bharat. In fact, even someone like Sheldon Pollock, who is projected as a sobering figure in the American Indology arena, especially in comparison with the likes of Wendy Doniger and Audrey Truschke, describes the Ramayana as a “hegemonic discourse” used to legitimise elite domination — specifically by kings and Brahmins — over the masses. He has also argued that the Ramayana’s portrayal of Ravan and the Rakshasas as “others” helped create an ideological template for later hostility towards Muslims.

It is against this larger socio-political and intellectual background that Bhagwat’s Madison Square Garden remarks should be analysed and understood. First, he was participating in an event centred on “Universal Oneness”. His speech naturally reflected that theme. Expecting him to use such an occasion to catalogue religious conflicts would be like looking for culinary advice in an economics textbook.
Second, he was speaking abroad and presenting a civilisational understanding of Bharat and Hinduism to an international audience. Swami Vivekananda’s Chicago address offers a useful historical parallel. Vivekananda spoke differently before Western audiences than he often did in Bharat because his audience, purpose and historical circumstances were different. Third, and most importantly, Bhagwat projected what he regards as the authentic civilisational ethos of Sanatana Dharma: inclusivity without uniformity, unity without erasure and respect for multiple paths without demanding that they become identical.

For decades, Bharat and its traditions have been filtered abroad through a familiar vocabulary: caste, communalism, majoritarianism and religious nationalism. Bhagwat’s intervention attempted to challenge that jaundiced gaze. It placed before an international audience an innately Indian civilisational proposition in which diversity need not be patronisingly tolerated, but genuinely respected and even cherished.

Mohan Bhagwat — first in New York and then in Toronto a day later — pitched “universal oneness”. Will the critics of the RSS do the same now?

(The writer is the author of ‘Bharat Rising: Dharma, Democracy, Diplomacy’ and ‘Eminent Distorians: Twists and Truths in Bharat’s History’. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Beyond SCO: Decoding PM Modi’s Uzbekistan outreach amid great power rivalry
editorials.passage:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Uzbekistan on his way to Kyrgyzstan to attend the 26th annual meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) is a significant bilateral diplomatic mission for India. The SCO meeting in Bishkek amidst current geopolitical challenges is crucial and will yet again witness Prime Minister Modi’s high-stakes interactions with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

However, New Delhi’s move to further deepen its strategic partnership with Uzbekistan, a key SCO member and a Central Asian power, is vital too. Like India, “strategic autonomy” and “multi-alignment” guide Uzbekistan’s foreign policy. It is the most populous country in the Central Asian region, is rich in key strategic minerals, is located between China, Russia, Iran, Afghanistan and the Caspian Sea, and is the hub of several connectivity projects.

More importantly, the economic transformation of the country since the current President, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, assumed power in 2016 has been remarkable. Russia, China and the United States have been consistently contesting for presence and influence in Uzbekistan. Even after it became independent in December 1991, Russian economic ties and strategic interests in Uzbekistan remain strong. Uzbekistan is an observer of the Russia-backed Eurasian Economic Union. China has emerged as the largest trading partner of this country and the biggest investor in the Uzbek economy, and Tashkent has willingly become part of China’s Belt and Road Initiative.

While the United States has been relatively slow in strengthening its influence in Uzbekistan, it certainly aspires to balance Great Power presence in Uzbekistan. Washington sought Uzbekistan’s help during the Global War against terrorism and used bases in the country during the NATO military intervention in Afghanistan. Uzbekistan, in fact, hosted the “Northern Distribution Network” for the supply of goods and materials to NATO forces.

The US strategic requirement coincided with Uzbekistan’s desire to follow a multi-alignment foreign policy to avoid domination by any single power. More recently, Uzbekistan entered into a critical-minerals partnership with the Trump Administration in February 2026. Uzbekistan also joined President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to address the issues of Gaza. Washington and Tashkent have reportedly agreed to implement an economic cooperation programme with a multi-year package of deals worth about $35 billion.

Significantly, India has systematically established a friendly bond with Uzbekistan over a decade, and Prime Minister Modi has not only visited Tashkent multiple times to bolster multifarious cooperation with that country but has also met the Uzbek President numerous times at multilateral forums, including the SCO and BRICS. The regular high-level exchanges of visits and dialogues between India and Uzbekistan are not limited to heads of government. Foreign Ministers, Defence Ministers, National Security Advisers and even Speakers of the respective legislatures of the two countries have interacted with each other on global, regional and bilateral issues.

India-Uzbekistan annual trade is more than a billion dollars, and the two countries intend to raise it to $5 billion by 2030. Although the current trade is much less than its potential, India is one of the top ten trading partners of Uzbekistan. Critical minerals, energy and digital integration between the two countries are expected to grow in the coming years. Indian investment in Uzbekistan is close to $1 billion, and during Prime Minister Modi’s visit in August 2026, it was announced that the target is to enhance mutual investment by about five times and bilateral trade by about ten times in the coming years.

India-Uzbekistan relations go much beyond high-level meetings and trade and investment cooperation. The two countries have wide-ranging cooperation on defence and security matters as well. The militaries of the two countries regularly hold joint exercises called “DUSTLIK”. The India-Uzbekistan Joint Working Group meeting on defence cooperation was held a few weeks before Prime Minister Modi’s recent visit to Tashkent.
Significantly, India and Uzbekistan maintain close cooperation in the fields of education and culture as well. Fifteen universities in Uzbekistan have set up India Studies Centres. Yoga and classical Indian dances are very popular in Uzbekistan. While the Indian diaspora population in Uzbekistan is more than 20,000, several times more people from the two countries are tourists who constitute a substantive group of contributors to the tourism industries.

Prime Minister Modi truly deserves the credit for making Uzbekistan an important strategic partner of India across a comprehensive range of sectors. That the two countries strongly believe in the principles of strategic autonomy and multi-alignment is crucial to maintaining enduring friendship and cooperation; and, by implication, their relationships with third countries will not be allowed to disrupt this bilateral strategic partnership.

(The writer is founder chairperson of Kalinga Institute of Indo-Pacific Studies and editor, ‘India Quarterly’. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Nepal Flash Flood Disaster: The Himalayan Crisis India and China Must Address
editorials.passage: Nepal is currently coping with a massive natural disaster near its border with China, and the scale of the death and destruction is catastrophic. On Wednesday, 26 August, a massive flash flood originated on the northern flank of Langtang Lirung (7,234m) in Nepal, after a rock and ice collapse triggered a huge debris flow down the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli river system. As of 30 August, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority has confirmed 734 dead and more than 3,000 missing in Nepal. More than 400 Indian nationals are also missing, including Kailash Mansarovar Yatra pilgrims.By Wednesday evening, the Rasuwagadhi crossing that links Nepal and Tibet had vanished. Social media was flooded with tragic images of the devastation. High-resolution images comparing April 2024 and 27 August 2026 showed the scale of the destruction: China-Nepal border infrastructure, the dry port, and the road, which is also the hydropower lifeline, were all reduced to rubble.Nepal Floods: China’s Tibet Grip Leaves a Dangerous Information Gap in HimalayasThis was not new. On 8 July 2025, the same river system, the Lhende Khola that becomes the Bhotekoshi, produced a flash flood after a supraglacial lake at 5,150 metres, 36km north of the border in Tibet, shrank from 0.74 sq km to 0.60 sq km in hours. That 2025 flood took the Miteri Friendship Bridge and left nine dead and 19 missing, including six Chinese nationals.At the time, Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, backed by ICIMOD (International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development), called it a supraglacial lake outburst.The 26 August tragedy, initially thought to be a quake, was caused by glacier ice plus rock collapse, causing a debris dam that led to a dam burst. International agencies initially misread this as an M4.4 quake and later revised it to an M5.2 glacial collapse.To compound the tragedy, on Friday, 28 August, a second threat was looming: the earlier debris created a barrier lake 10km upstream, holding roughly 1,000 Olympic swimming pools’ worth of water. It briefly overflowed, forcing a second evacuation in Rasuwa and sending fresh panic down to Bidur Municipality.Geologists say such barrier lakes from ice-rock avalanches are now the classic Himalayan secondary disaster. Nepal’s Flash Floods Show the Devastating Power of ‘Cascading Hazards’Nepal’s response since 2015 has significantly changed, and this is the first positive lesson. In 2015, Kathmandu needed foreign assistance for search and rescue (SAR) operations. This week, to its credit, Nepal mobilised within 24 hours. The Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and NDRRMA evacuated more than 485 people and deployed two Army helicopters for SAR, with Prime Minister Balen Shah holding coordination meetings while district disaster committees issued downstream alerts for the Trishuli. Intrepid Nepalese helicopter pilots are to be commended for their courage and professional acumen in launching some very hair-raising rescue operations.On 28 August, Nepal’s Foreign Ministry declined offers of foreign rescue help, saying, “our agencies are doing it.” That decision, deemed controversial given that 540 foreigners were missing, reflected a new confidence in Nepal’s national capacity, carefully built up over the last decade. However, Nepal has since requested specialised foreign technical equipment that India and China have provided.But two things have not changed since 2015, and both were revealed on 8 July 2025 and again now.First, the absence of sustained, trans-boundary cryosphere data. The Lhende catchment is transnational by definition, and there is no robust regional data sharing. Instead, data sharing remains transactional. India and China both suspend hydrological data when relations sour, as they did after Doklam in 2017 and Galwan in 2020.Alas, the cost is paid by Nepal's local residents, tourists and pilgrims. If the European Alps have taught the world anything, it is that specific mass-balance monitoring (continuous, per unit area) is more important than absolute loss rates.The Alps have a far more negative specific balance than the Himalaya; the Himalaya’s danger is not uniform melting, but episodic, compound failures: rock and ice collapse plus glacial lakes triggering a quake.This cannot be tracked with rainfall radars and needs more refined, open-source cryosphere data that is glacier-specific.Second, the blame game that followed was reminiscent of COVID.Last year, in July 2025, a Nepali minister suggested China was hiding information about the lake breach; Beijing pushed back. This week saw the same script being pulled out. Chinese media called Nepali warnings “fake news” and blamed a Nepal-side quake; sections of the Nepali press accused China of withholding early warning about the barrier lake. Doubts were expressed about the origin of the current tragedy. Was it Nepal or Tibet/China? However, this spat has since been resolved, and President Xi Jinping has extended both condolences and rescue assistance.Assam Needs a Climate Mobility Plan, Not Just Flood ReliefAgainst this tragic backdrop, India and China have a chance to demonstrate collective leadership in enabling the Global South, and the timing matters.  On 12 September, New Delhi hosts the BRICS Summit with expanded members, including key Himalayan and riverine states. New Delhi has pitched this summit as one about inclusive growth and disaster resilience.The most appropriate deliverable would be a joint India-China-Nepal announcement of a Himalayan Glacial Hazard Early Warning System, with a standing protocol for cryosphere and hydrological data, glacial lake area change and real-time river levels from Tibet to the Ganga plain – not as a goodwill gesture after a disaster, but as a regional obligation.Further, the region needs a second deliverable: a pre-authorised Himalayan HADR compact. South Asia has the SAARC Disaster Management Centre in Gujarat; ASEAN has the AHA (ASEAN Humanitarian Assistance) Centre in Jakarta, but the India-Nepal-China border has no similar rapid-reaction, cross-border protocol.What is needed is an agreement where satellite tasking, helicopter airlifts and search teams can move within six hours of a glacial event without waiting for diplomatic notes, especially when the very infrastructure for cooperation – friendship bridges, dry ports and power lines – is washed away.The flood of 26 August could not have been anticipated by rainfall forecasting alone. Hopefully, the next one can be better tracked and better responded to if hydrological and cryosphere (glacier-related) data is treated as a public good, not as leverage.In the interim, prayers for those still missing and deepest condolences to the families of the bereaved.(C Uday Bhaskar is a leading expert on strategic affairs. He is currently Director, Society for Policy Studies. This is an opinion piece. All views expressed are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for them.)
